title: The Fathers on Proverbs
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (emails of 8 and 9 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 9 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: Solomon, son of David, points to the Savior, also called son of David, who reigns in Israel over those who are truly Israel.
comments.comment: Proverbs of Solomon, son of David. The Savior too is called son of David. This peaceable Savior of ours, who came from David seed according to the flesh, reigned in Israel. That is why, as he completed the economy for human beings, he was also labeled: This is the King of the Jews. Jews are Israel — those over whom the peaceable Savior reigns as over people who see clearly — if they are truly Israel. For not all who are Abraham seed are also children, when they do not do Abraham works.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A proverb signifies intelligible things through sensible things, Israel's kingdom is spiritual knowledge, and wisdom and instruction are knowledge and moderation of the passions.
comments.comment: A proverb is a word signifying intelligible things through sensible things. … The kingdom of Israel is spiritual knowledge containing discourses concerning God and incorporeal and corporeal things and judgment and providence, or revealing the contemplation concerning ethics, physics, and theology. For this reason he says: ‘He made instruction and wisdom reign in Israel, to know instruction and wisdom’ (Prov 1:2). And wisdom is the knowledge of corporeal and incorporeal things and of the judgment and providence contemplated in them; but instruction is moderation of the passions, contemplated with regard to the passionate or irrational part of the soul.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the words proverb, wisdom and instruction in plain terms.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Wisdom is knowledge of divine and human affairs, and to know it is to know Christ, the power and wisdom of God.
comments.comment: To know wisdom and training. Wisdom is knowledge that takes hold of divine and human affairs. Some say it is a vapor of God power and a pure outflow of the Almighty glory; nothing dark falls into it. It is a radiance of everlasting light, a spotless mirror of God working, and an image of his goodness. Whoever knows wisdom works knows these: that radiance, that spotless mirror, that image of goodness. And that is nothing other than to know the Son of God love, and the Wisdom who is Christ. For Christ is God power and God wisdom. This is not unveiled from flesh and blood, but from the heavenly Father. Whoever also knows the science of the divine oracles — of the Law and the prophets, of the Gospels and the apostles — knows wisdom.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what wisdom means in this verse in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The criterion for judging is right and unperverted; we have three: sensation, word, mind.
comments.comment: ‘To direct judgment’ shows that the criterion is right and unperverted. There are three criteria in us: sensation, word, and mind — sensation of sensible things, word of names and sayings and things spoken, mind of intelligible things.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Shrewdness can be praised, as when Luke has the steward praised for sharpness of mind.
comments.comment: [Of 'shrewdness':] And if Luke says he praised the steward of injustice, he stretched the word, taking the praise for shrewdness and for sharpness of mind. That seems to show also in the serpent was shrewdest of all the beasts, and in the saying be shrewd as serpents — as if not inexperienced in the serpent tricks.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The name of cunning is used in Scripture both in praise, as in wisdom's gift of cunning to the guileless, and in reproach, as when the serpent deceived Eve in his cunning.
comments.comment: To know that in the divine scripture the name of cunning is placed not only in a reproachful sense but also in a praiseworthy one. For when it is said regarding wisdom, 'that I might give cunning to the guileless' (Proverbs 1:4), it is clear, as it speaks of prudence and a praiseworthy deed; for such a thing is given by wisdom. And again: 'the cunning one was averted from coming evils' (Jon 3:4), which indicates a sensible action, which is accomplished toward him in the manner of repentance when the onset of evils is proven, as the Ninevites did, fleeing the threat; for the wrath is dispersed by this repentance. That cunning is also placed reproachfully is shown in: 'I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve in his cunning, your thoughts might be made frivolous' (2 Cor 11:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains clearly that 'cunning' in the verse is praiseworthy prudence, while it can also be blamed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The word 'shrewdness' is in a sense neutral, with a blamed kind and a good kind that Wisdom promises to the innocent.
comments.comment: Leaven, then, would be a type of shrewdness, and not by any means only of the kind that is blamed, but of the other kind too, I mean the good kind that is praised, which the word of Wisdom also promises to give to the innocent (Proverbs 1:4). For the word ‘shrewdness’ is, in a sense, neutral.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: A parable is speech about something that did not happen according to the letter yet could happen, and it points figuratively to realities, like the sower who went out to sow.
comments.comment: He will also understand a parable and a dark saying, sayings of the wise and riddles. Let us see how these differ. First, what is a parable, from the Gospel materials we have? Others used the name, and Matthew writes: On that day Jesus went out of the house, sat beside the sea, and the whole crowd stood on the shore, and he spoke many things to them in parables: Look, a sower went out to sow. A parable, then, is speech as about something that happened, which did not happen according to the letter yet could happen, and which points figuratively to realities by transferring what the parable says. For the sower went out did not happen as history happens; yet it could happen according to the letter.
comments.selected_reason: Defines a parable clearly, with an example from the Gospels.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus goes out of the house to speak parables to those outside and goes into the house to explain them to his disciples.
comments.comment: I think that when Jesus speaks in parables to those outside — to whom, being outside, it was not given to know the mysteries of God kingdom — he has gone out of the house, as Matthew reports, and not without reason when he writes that on that day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea. Toward those who could not enter the house but stood outside it, it was fitting that he go out. That Matthew intends this is clear from what follows: leaving the crowds, he entered his house and opens the parable to the disciples. Watch how he speaks to the crowds in parables and says nothing to them without a parable — as he still does, for crowds cannot take an interpretation of parables.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Crowds who hear a parable never stop to ask for its meaning, but the disciples follow Jesus into the house to learn it.
comments.comment: I also try to hear more deeply: The disciples came and said, Why do you speak to them in parables? and Leaving the crowds he came into his house; and his disciples came saying, Explain the parable to us. Crowds who hear a parable never even pause over it as needing explanation. Disciples see that he speaks in parables to crowds because they are outside; they follow Jesus as he leaves the crowds; they see they can learn the parables nowhere else than by entering Jesus house; so they enter, come to him, and say, Explain to us the parable we want to learn. That is the parable.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A dark saying is a Scripture so deliberately obscure that no one can catch even a casual sense of it without much hard examination, as in Psalm 32, 'my bones grew old'.
comments.comment: Next is the dark saying. In the Scriptures some things are said so deliberately dark that no one can catch even a casual sense in them without much hard examination — muddled in phrasing, in thought, and in how the wording is put together. I take that to be what a book calls a dark saying. An example from the Psalms, from Psalm 32: Because I was silent, my bones grew old, and what follows. Of ordinary thought you can grasp the letter, as we will show; of a dark saying, not even that. Compare Isaiah: Woe, wings of a land of ships beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, sending hostages by sea and papyrus letters on the water. Clarifying each of these and lighting its darkness by interpretation is not for this moment, lest we digress too far. It is enough to clarify the psalm saying somehow. As long as I cried out hymning God and spoke of God all day, nothing in me grew old; I was being made new. But when I fell idle from theology and was silent, oldness sank as far as my bones and what seemed firmest in me. Then followed Your hand heavy on me night and day, and so from earlier oversight your weighted hand was turned into my misery. I deserved it: a thorn was fixed in me when cares, or wealth, or life pleasures held me. That the prophet meant this is clear from what follows: I made known my sin, and so on. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what a dark saying is and works through a clear example.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The hearer should understand the sayings of the other wise too, so that the mind is not caught by persuasive falsehoods and can free those who are.
comments.comment:
[On 'sayings of the wise':] Why should the hearer understand the sayings of the blessed wise, yet not stretch to the words of the other wise, and have a mind smaller than the mind of this world wise, unable to follow what they say?

Is it not as with the eye, whose work is not only to see what is in order but also what is otherwise — or as craft wishes in such cases — so also with the mind: its work is to contemplate both thoughts that hit and thoughts that miss, so that it is not caught by the persuasiveness in falsehoods, and so that it can rescue those who are caught, if it also understands the sayings of the other wise wherever they play at wisdom, how they reason falsely, how the sophism is loosed, and how the false reasoning is exposed.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A riddle is an extended account of things as if they happened that did not and cannot happen, yet which signify something unspeakable in hiddenness, as in the trees choosing a king in Judges.
comments.comment: It remains to say what riddles are. I take a riddle to be an extended account about things as if they happened that did not happen and cannot happen, yet that signify something unspeakable in hiddenness. Sample from Judges: The trees went to anoint a king over themselves. Which three fruit trees — fig, vine, olive — refused to reign over trees unworthy of their kingship, and what is the thorny bramble that sends fire from itself to eat Lebanon cedars — the wise person sees, referring these to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and the bramble to the opposing one. In Kingdoms there is such a riddle too: The thorn in Lebanon sent to the Cedar in Lebanon, saying, Give your daughter to my son as wife, and what follows. In the prophets you also find riddles, as in Ezekiel: The great eagle, long-winged, long in stretch, full of feathers, and what follows.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Mystical things were set forth through riddles, allegories, dark sayings and parables so that those who labor for virtue and truth might examine and find.
comments.comment: The prophets, then, in accordance with the will of God, spoke without any concealment whatever their hearers could usefully understand at once and whatever helped to correct their conduct. But what was more mystical, more for the eyes of the initiated, and bound up with a contemplation beyond what the common ear can take in, they set forth “through riddles” (Numbers 12:8), through allegories, through what are called dark sayings, and through what are named parables or proverbs (Proverbs 1:6). They did this so that those who do not shrink from toil, but take on every labour for the sake of virtue and truth, might examine and find, and, having found, might put what they found to use as reason requires.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse names riddles and dark sayings: they were meant to be examined and found.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Beginning' can mean the base from which something comes, as reverence is a base for perfection.
comments.comment: “Beginning” is also used of that from which something comes, as the foundation is in a house and the keel in a ship, according to what is said: “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Proverbs 1:7; cf. Psalm 111:10 LXX). For reverence is like a base and a pedestal for perfection.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why fear of the Lord is called the beginning of wisdom.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: The crown of graces is the circle of the virtues; the neck is the mind.
comments.comment: A crown of graces: the circuit of the virtues, because they are bound to one another. A golden collar about your neck: he calls the golden collar the surrounding radiance and circular gleam of the divine oracles, and he calls the neck the mind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the crown and collar in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Cast your lot among us' is the call of those who would kill the heir, to leave one's way of life.
comments.comment: Those who said This is the heir; come, let us kill him so the inheritance may be ours would also say this. Cast your lot among us: leave that way of life, be with us, keep sabbath with us, keep the unleavened rites with us, and the other law observances. For they themselves share in the murder.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God gives good things and we are the causes of evils, and to complete lawless deeds is to fill the measure of their fathers.
comments.comment: God gives good things; we are causes of evils — of things that harm. You would also say this of the Jews who shared in blood, both of the prophets and of Christ himself. These are the roads of all who complete lawless deeds. To complete, I think, is not merely to do something, but to fill the measure of their fathers, and to be liable for every blood from Abel to Zechariah.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Wisdom is hymned once it obtains a going-out.
comments.comment: Wisdom is hymned in goings-out. Kept silent by a wise man, it is not hymned; once it obtains a going-out, it is hymned.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Whoever calls upon Christ, understanding who he is, calls upon wisdom and every virtue, if not with lips then with practices.
comments.comment: For there will be a time when you call upon me. As Lord we call upon the wisdom that is Christ. So whoever calls upon Christ, if he understands who he is, calls upon wisdom, understanding, sanctification, righteousness, and every virtue — if not with lips, then with practices. But let us not become the sort who call, only for him not to listen.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what it means to call upon wisdom.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Evil men seek wisdom only to hide it and make it vanish, whereas those eager to become wise pursue it.
comments.comment: For Wisdom says: 'Evil men will seek me and will not find me' (Proverbs 1:28). The evil men seek wisdom only to hide it and make it vanish, as much as it reaches them. But those eager to become wise do not seek wisdom in this way, but they pursue it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what it means that evil men seek wisdom and do not find it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Hiding the commandment seeks to escape notice, not glory.
comments.comment: If, receiving a saying of my commandment, you hide it with yourself. Someone hides it not for empty glory, but eager to escape notice.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what hiding the commandment means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Each person gives his voice to something, but the blessed one gives it to the Lord and seeks wisdom as one seeks silver.
comments.comment: And give your voice to understanding. Each person gives his voice to something — to anger speaking its lines, or to grief, or to sexual immorality. The blessed one dedicates his whole voice to the Lord, so that whatever he speaks may be wisdom. As another seeks silver, seek wisdom that way, becoming a lover of silver in this.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what giving one's voice to understanding means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Many steps lead to understanding the fear of the Lord, which is itself unclear.
comments.comment: Then you will understand fear of the Lord. See after how many steps we will understand that fear; it too is unclear, as simpler people show: some fear the Lord where they need not, and do not fear where they ought.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the fear of the Lord must be learned.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: There is a divine sense, found by the blessed man, with its own sight, hearing, taste, smell and touch, by which the prophets saw, heard and touched the Word.
comments.comment: There is, as Scripture has named it, a divine sense, general in kind, which only the blessed man finds even now, according to what is said in Solomon too: “You will find a divine sense” (Proverbs 2:5). This sense has its kinds: a sight naturally able to see things higher than bodies, among which the cherubim or the seraphim are shown (Ezekiel 10:1; Isaiah 6:2); a hearing that receives voices whose being is not in the air; a taste that feeds on living bread, which has come down from heaven and gives life to the world (John 6:33, 51); so too a smell that smells such things as Paul means when he speaks of being “the aroma of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:15); and a touch, by which John says he has handled with his hands “the Word of life” (1 John 1:1). The blessed prophets found this divine sense. They saw in a divine way and heard in a divine way, and tasted and smelled in the same way, by a sense that, if I may so name it, is not of the senses; and they touched the Word with faith, so that an outflow from him came to them to heal them. In this way they saw what they record that they saw, and heard what they say they heard, and had the like experiences as they wrote of them, eating the “roll” of a book that was given to them (Ezekiel 2:9–3:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains clearly what the 'divine sense' of the verse is.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Understanding is twofold, of the hands and of mind and hand, and the practical kind is shown in the understanding of the good in all who practice it.
comments.comment: For the nature of understanding is twofold: one is of the hands, the other of mind and hand; for understanding, which is called along with wisdom, comes into being through the mind. Concerning this it is said, 'The Lord gives wisdom, and from his face knowledge and understanding' (Proverbs 2:6). But the one of the hands, being practical and productive, is shown in the understanding of the good in all those who practice it. For the understanding that is practiced is practical knowledge; and by this the teacher guides certain ones who are not so much benefited by words.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those alien to the Church promise one thing at the start and another at the end.
comments.comment: Let a bad counsel not overtake you. Those alien to the Church promise one thing at the start and another at the end: first they pull people from idolatry toward the Creator; then they change and set aside the Old Scripture, opposing elemental youth. With church teachers the ends agree with the first elements.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To forget the law is not to live by it, and to keep God's words is to do them, for doers of the law are justified.
comments.comment: 'My son, do not forget my commandments; let your heart keep my words' (Prov 3:1). If this one forgets the law, the one not living according to it, this one remembers the law; but if this one keeps the words of God, the one doing them, this one destroys them, the one not willing to do them; 'for the hearers of the law are not righteous before God, he says, but the doers of the law will be justified' (Rom 2:13).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The words of God's wisdom announce unlying knowledge after the commands of the law, and whoever keeps the laws will take up wisdom.
comments.comment: … Let your heart keep my words. After the commands and bans of God law, the words of God wisdom announce unlying knowledge of the things that are. Such also is Out of Zion will go the law, and a word of the Lord out of Jerusalem. Whoever keeps the laws will take up wisdom. Sow for yourselves righteousness; harvest into a time of life. Then next to the practical comes: Light for yourselves a light of knowledge. Provide good things before the Lord and humans. If you do what you practice in wisdom, you will be a son of God, as it says: You made all things in wisdom.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We must trust God with the whole heart and not be puffed up by the wisdom of God, which is what makes our paths straight.
comments.comment: 'Be of good trust with all your heart in God; but do not be proud of your own wisdom' (Prov 3:5-7). 'Do not be puffed up,' he says, 'having acquired the wisdom of God.' Because he says here the wisdom of God and not the human wisdom, by which he demonstrates: 'for in all your ways you will know her, so that she may make your paths straight' (Prov 3:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verses ask and why the wisdom meant is God's own.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: When the powers of the soul receive care, each of them, memory, sight, desire and reckoning, will say the greatest things to the Lord.
comments.comment: 'Then there will be healing to your body and care to your bones' (Prov 3:8). When the powers of the soul receive care, they will say the greatest things: 'Lord, who is like you? For all, he says, my bones will say: Lord, Lord, who is like you?' Because the mnemonic power of the soul, receiving care, will certainly say, 'I remembered God and was glad.' Similarly, the optic power will say, 'I understood your works and was astonished.' Likewise also the desiring power: 'Lord, all my desire is against you.' And the calculating power will also say, 'I considered the days of old.' According to these things, it will happen also to the other powers.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A gift from injustice and robbery should not be brought, and wealth from righteous labors that does not feed the poor is reckoned as robbery.
comments.comment: Therefore the Proverb advises: “Honor the Lord from your righteous labors, and offer him firstfruits from your fruits of righteousness” (Proverbs 3:9). For if you are about to bring an offering to God from injustice and robbery, it is better neither to acquire such a possession nor to bring an offering from it. For a pure gift will carry the prayer, as it is written: “The prayers of the upright are acceptable to him” (Proverbs 15:8). And again, if you acquire from righteous labors but do not bring offerings to God from which the poor are fed, it will be reckoned to you as robbery.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what honoring the Lord from righteous labors requires.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: People of old honored God with sacrifices of oxen and frankincense, but those in Christ honor him with spiritual and holy offerings in worship in spirit and truth.
comments.comment: … we must offer to God, like a sweet fragrance and as a debt we owe, a way of life fitting for saints and the glories of an outstanding life. You have learned from one of the saints, who wrote: ‘Honor the Lord from your just labors, and offer him firstfruits from your fruits of righteousness’ (Proverbs 3:9). For the people of old thought they honored him with sacrifices of oxen and with frankincense, since that was the road of life under the law. But we, who are now in Christ through faith, are going by the better and more excellent path, and we shall offer God worship in spirit and truth (John 4:23–24), making every effort, as it were, to be able to carry out nobly what we ought, and honoring God with spiritual and holy offerings.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: Honor means a gift, from just labors and not from seizure and greed, and everything done toward God is a gift: virtues, firstfruits, prayer and psalms.
comments.comment: Honor the Lord from your just labors. Divine Scripture customarily takes honor for a gift … He said from just labors so it would not be from seizure and greed. Let no one hesitate to give; after the Gospel widow who threw her whole living and was justified — not beside those who threw from seizure, but beside those who threw from surplus — no one has a defense. Everything is a gift toward God: works of temperance and the other virtues. Give firstfruits from every offspring to Church and poor; rising from sleep give prayer as firstfruit to God; give a firstfruit of words — psalms. Then it will be said to you: Blessed are your storehouses and your leftovers — meaning the things of the soul.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'honor' means here and what the firstfruits are.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and a saint ready for the lashes is like a patient telling a wise physician that he is ready for the incision.
comments.comment: But also that which is said in Proverbs, 'Whom the Lord loves He disciplines, and scourges every son whom He receives' (Proverbs 3:12), subjects the mind to the same. And one of the saints, having this readiness and speaking boldly, offering words of repentance to God, said, 'I am ready for the lashes'; for I know that it happens profitably from You, just as one says to a wise physician, 'I am even ready for the incision, being confident in your skill.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: If some things are inflicted by the Lord we should offer him patience and rejoice in his chastisement, for Scripture says he corrects those he loves.
comments.comment: But if we believe some things are inflicted by the Lord, to whom should we offer patience more than to the Lord? Moreover, he teaches us to rejoice and be glad in the condescension of divine chastisement. Scripture says, "I correct those whom I love" (Proverbs 3:12). O blessed servant, whose correction the Lord presses upon, whom he deigns to be angry with, whom he does not deceive by concealing his admonition!
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why a believer should take divine correction with patience.
comments.author: Tertullian

comments.capsule: Nothing evil opposes wisdom: a mind occupied with its theorems cannot be given unclean thoughts by the demons unless they are permitted.
comments.comment: Something more precious than costly stones is; nothing evil opposes it. Toward wisdom alone, the demons are unable to cast thoughts into the heart of the one having become wise, if they are not permitted; for the mind, being occupied with the theorems of wisdom, becomes unfit for unclean thoughts. A pure mind approaches wisdom; but the unclean will be distanced from it.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Wisdom's right hand is knowledge of divine things bringing eternal life; her left, of human things bringing riches and glory.
comments.comment: It also says elsewhere [than in the Song of Songs], 'Length of life and years of life are in the right hand of Wisdom, and in her left are riches and glory' (Proverbs 3:16). Her right hand, then, is the knowledge of divine things, from which comes eternal life; her left is the knowledge of human things, from which come riches and glory.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the right and left hand of Wisdom in plain terms.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: Fragments on the Song of Songs

comments.capsule: If the tree of life is the wisdom of God, Adam was justly prevented from grasping it, for wisdom will not enter a craftless soul.
comments.comment: It is a tree of life to all those holding fast to it. Adam is prevented from partaking of this tree after the transgression, if 'a tree of life grows from the fruits of righteousness.' But if the tree of life is the wisdom of God, he is justly prevented from grasping this tree; 'for into a craftless soul, he says, wisdom will not enter.'
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Paul's breadth, height, depth and length are symbols of rational natures divided by worlds and bodies.
comments.comment:
God established the world by wisdom.

The earth: and the holy Paul named the breadth there; and the heavens being called height in his epistle to the Ephesians; and the so-called tropical abysses he names depth; and the cloud-formed mists he calls length. All these are symbols of rational natures, divided by worlds and bodies according to the analogy of their state.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The faithful soul is earth founded by wisdom, and as it advances it is worked into a heaven, a dwelling of angels.
comments.comment: God founded earth by wisdom. The faithful soul too is earth, bearing fruit a hundredfold. From that richness, which is wisdom, she becomes wise, as God founds her upon it. He seats the introduction of teaching for her, fixing it from wisdom, and as she always advances he works her into a heaven — a most pure creature, a dwelling of angels and thinking essences. Taking perception of what is, and contemplating the exactness of affairs, she begins to divide and cut them through.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Will' is movement concerning practical things, 'understanding' concerning theoretical things, and 'neck' the soul that bore the yoke.
comments.comment: He speaks of 'will' as the movement concerning practical things; 'understanding' as that concerning theoretical things; 'neck' he says of the same soul, which bore the yoke of the Lord (Matt 11:29-30). Just as the neck encircles the breast-bands, so the soul carries the things of God in the kingdom, just as it does his commandments here.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Neck' means the soul that has borne the yoke of the Lord, and 'stumbling block' means an impure thought or a false knowledge.
comments.comment: ‘That your soul may live, and that there may be grace around your neck’ (Proverbs 3:22): ‘Neck’ he says of the soul that has borne the yoke of the Lord. ‘That all your ways may go in confidence in peace, and that your foot may not stumble’ (Prov 3:2, 23): ‘Stumbling block’ is an impure thought of rational nature or a false knowledge.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the picture words of the verses in plain terms.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Almsgiving removes the fearful fantasies of the night, and so do gentleness, lack of anger and patience, which restrain the disturbed passion.
comments.comment: ‘If you sit, you shall be without fear; and if you sleep, you shall sleep sweetly, and you shall not be afraid of a falling terror or the coming of the impulses of the ungodly’ (Prov 3:2, 24-25). From this we know that almsgiving removes fearful fantasies occurring to us in the night. Gentleness, lack of anger, and patience also do the same, restraining the passion that is prone to be disturbed, if indeed fearful phantoms are wont to arise from the disturbance of the passion.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Enmity toward the neighbor works some evil.
comments.comment: ‘Do not envy a man without cause, lest he work evil against you’ (Proverbs 3:30): This enmity toward the neighbor works some evil.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: By adding 'of wicked men', the verse shows that serious men too may be a reproach, as when the disciples rejoice at being reproached.
comments.comment: Indeed, in the writing of Proverbs, it is said to the wise man: 'Do not acquire the reproach of wicked men' (Proverbs 3:31). By adding 'of wicked men,' it showed that even serious men are a reproach. For instance, the disciples rejoice when they are reproached. These are not the reproaches for which the apostles are refuted, namely, the reproaches of wicked men.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even prosperous things are cursed for the ungodly, and even humble things are blessed for the righteous.
comments.comment: … For the ungodly, even the prosperous things are cursed; but for the righteous, even the most humble things are blessed. He calls the powers of the rational soul a 'house'; and 'dwellings' the powers of the spirited and the appetitive; for within them the irrational suffer passions.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The curse is the ignorance of the Lord in the souls of the ungodly, and the Lord resists the proud as humility, while the wise inherit knowledge and the ungodly honor ignorance.
comments.comment: ‘The curse of God in the houses of the ungodly; but the dwellings of the righteous are blessed’ (Proverbs 3:33): ‘The ignorance of the Lord in the souls of the ungodly; but the knowledge of God in the souls of the righteous’ (Proverbs 3:33). ‘The Lord resists the proud, but gives grace to the lowly’ (Prov 3:34): Just as the Lord resists the unrighteous as righteousness, and the liars as truth, so also he resists the proud as humility. ‘The wise shall inherit glory; but the ungodly have exalted dishonor’ (Prov 3:35): The wise shall inherit knowledge; but the ungodly have honored ignorance.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the curse, the grace and the glory of these verses are.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The law is named a 'good gift' in contrast to the unjust gifts, which are the commands of the evil one, and he who transgresses it abandons it.
comments.comment: ‘For I will give you a good gift’ (Proverbs 4:2): It should be noted here that he names the law a ‘good gift’ because the one receiving gifts in his lap unjustly is not being guided straight. For there, the commands of the evil one are called unjust gifts, which the mind receiving them is not guided straight in its ways. ‘Do not abandon my law’ (Proverbs 4:2): He who transgresses it abandons the law.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Wisdom reveals her own beauty only to her lovers, so the unjust are blind to the beauty of righteousness.
comments.comment: The unjust are blind to the beauty of righteousness and do not see clearly the dignity and grace of the words about it. But the one who has chosen these words and wished to belong to them—this person alone is established in understanding, because wisdom reveals her own beauty only to her lovers, as it is written: “Love her, and she will honor you; honor her, that she may embrace you” (Proverbs 4:6, 8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why wisdom is shown only to those who love her.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The engravings of wisdom are the virtues which exalt the knowledge of God.
comments.comment: Engrave her, and she will exalt you. If it is within our power to engrave wisdom, and the virtues are within our power, then the engravings here signify the virtues which exalt the knowledge of God.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The honor of wisdom is keeping the commandments; wisdom is Christ.
comments.comment: … honor of wisdom is the keeping of the commandments; but wisdom is Christ, whose bride is the soul honoring him through virtues, which shall be received by him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what honoring wisdom means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The knowledge of God is a crown of grace protecting us from passionate thoughts and false knowledge.
comments.comment: That you may give a crown of graces to your head, and a crown of splendor may protect you; the knowledge of God is a crown of grace and a crown of splendor, which also protects us from every passionate thought and every rejected false knowledge.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the crown of grace is.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The many paths of life lead into the one path, 'I am the way'.
comments.comment: Listen, son, and receive my words, and the years of your life shall be multiplied, so that many paths of life may become yours. These many paths lead into one path which said, 'I am the way' (John 14:6). The virtues have spoken of many paths that lead to the knowledge of Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the many paths of life are.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The army's place is wickedness and false knowledge.
comments.comment: In whatever place they may encamp, do not go there; but turn away from them and deviate. The place of this army is wickedness and false knowledge.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Sleep is taken from the impious, for the Lord gives sleep to his beloved, and the demons are not even able to sleep.
comments.comment: For they shall never sleep unless they do evil; sleep is taken away from them, they do not sleep. If the Lord gives sleep to his beloved, the impious are not his beloved; the Lord does not give sleep to the impious. From this it is also possible to show that the demons are not even able to sleep.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The army of the opposing power is nourished by impiety and lawlessness.
comments.comment: For these feed on the grain of impiety; and they get drunk on lawless wine. From this we know what the army of the opposing power is nourished by; for, he says, the grain is impiety and the wine is lawlessness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the bread and wine of wickedness mean.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Our virtues illuminate us until the sun of righteousness shines his own day.
comments.comment: But the paths of the righteous shine similarly with light; they go forward and illuminate, until the day is perfected. Our virtues go forward and illuminate us, until the sun of righteousness shines his own day upon us.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the shining path of the righteous.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The impious do not even know that they act lawlessly, the mark of ultimate folly.
comments.comment: But the paths of the impious are dark; they do not know how they stumble. The impious do not even know the way in which they sin, nor do they know the cause from where they stumble, but they do not even know this, that they act lawlessly, which is the mark of ultimate folly.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the darkness of the wicked's way.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The springs to be guarded are the virtues, which generate the knowledge of Christ.
comments.comment: So that your springs may not fail you, guard them in your heart. He calls the virtues 'springs,' from which the living water is generated, which is the knowledge of Christ. And David says: 'The springs of the waters appeared' (Psalm 18:15).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the springs are.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The springs of life are the virtues, from which comes the knowledge of Christ.
comments.comment: And the springs of life are the virtues, from which the living water is (John 4:14), namely the knowledge of Christ. To the one progressing according to wisdom, many springs become, and not only one; but according to the abundance of virtues. To those who guard these exhortations, he says, they become life; these are the contest.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Keeping the heart means letting no demon set foot on our ruling faculty.
comments.comment: Knowing these things, and others like them, we wish to keep the commandment spoken in a mystical sense: “Keep your heart with all watchfulness” (Proverbs 4:23), so that none of the demons may set foot on our ruling faculty, and no spirit of the opposing powers may turn our imagination to what it wishes.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what keeping the heart means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The crooked mouth and deceitful lips mean deceitful use of the members and boastful speech.
comments.comment: … For it is not necessary to consider the members of the body being destroyed, but their deceitful use and their boastful speech; for even in Proverbs it is said: 'Remove from yourself a crooked mouth and long deceitful lips from you' (Proverbs 4:24).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Dispassionate thoughts and true doctrines mean seeing uprightly.
comments.comment: Let your eyes see uprightly; and let your eyelids be righteous. Those who have dispassionate thoughts and true doctrines, these see uprightly.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: What the eye is to the body the mind is to the soul, lit by divine light, and it keeps from missing right doctrine.
comments.comment: For what the eye is to the earthly body, the mind may be called in the soul. It is lit up by the divine light, it opens its eyes to that pure beauty itself, and with the fine and nimble movements, as it were, of its thoughts it springs up readily toward exact belief, and knows how to keep from missing right doctrine. This, I think, is what is said in the Proverbs: ‘Let your eyes look straight, and let your eyelids nod toward what is just’ (Proverbs 4:25).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what looking straight means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The foot is a symbol of walking straight in one's paths, so we should walk well along the path to all that pleases God.
comments.comment: For this reason the hand also was sanctified, which points to active work, and the foot as well, a clear symbol of walking straight in one’s paths (Exodus 29:20). For we ought to take pride in holy works and walk well along the path that leads to everything pleasing to God, as is sung in the Psalms, ‘And I turned my feet to your testimonies’ (Psalm 119:59), or as the book of Proverbs says, ‘Make straight paths for your feet, and direct your ways’ (Proverbs 4:26).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: Turning to the right or to the left is forbidden, for both excess and deficiency are evils, such as stinginess and profligacy.
comments.comment: Both, indeed, are forbidden, the divine word says: 'Make straight paths for your feet, and direct your ways. Do not turn to the right or to the left' (Proverbs 4:26-27), neither into excesses nor into deficiencies; for both are evils. Of freedom—and this is the social choice—when it is lacking, the well-named deviation is stinginess, which is thought to be right, while profligacy is the consuming of resources not on what is necessary and as it should be, but upon the prey of shameful pleasures.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Virtue is a mean, so 'right' here names what only appears right through pleasures.
comments.comment: Do not turn to the right nor to the left; but turn your foot from the evil way. For virtue is a mean; therefore they say that courage is between rashness and cowardice. Now, 'right' names not those which are naturally right, but those things which appear to be right because of pleasures; …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why neither right nor left is allowed.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The good draws a person upward, while folly drags down those who choose it.
comments.comment: And since by nature the good is upward-tending and the bad pulls downward those who use it voluntarily—'for the feet of folly bring down those who use it after death into Hades' (Proverbs 5:5)—the bad is indeed below, but those using virtue attain to the things above …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why folly leads downward to Hades, in plain terms.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: There was a time without evil and there will be again, but virtue never ceases, and mercy is its best seed.
comments.comment: I was for a little while in all evil in the midst of a church and a synagogue. There was a time when there was no evil and there shall be a time when there shall be no evil; but there was not a time when there was no virtue, nor shall there be a time when there shall be no virtue, for the seeds of virtue are unceasing. And this one also persuades me, having been for a little while and not perfectly in all evil, even the rich man being judged in Hades because of evil and pitying his brothers. But to show mercy happens to be the most beautiful seed of virtue.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Knowledge is a cistern, then a fountain as one advances.
comments.comment: Knowledge is both a cistern and a fountain; to those coming to the virtues it is a cistern, but to those perfected by them, a fountain.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Knowledge seems a deep well to those approaching virtue, but is a spring to the pure.
comments.comment: Drink waters from your own vessels and from your own wells, a spring. Knowledge is both a well and a spring. To those approaching virtues, it seems to be a deep well, but to the impassive and the pure, a spring. So also the Savior 'was sitting by the well, it was about the sixth hour' (John 4:6). And the Samaritan woman calls the well herself: 'Lord, for you have no bucket and the well is deep' (John 4:11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the well and the spring of the verse, with a Gospel parallel a reader can follow.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The righteous dig wells to find the spring within, and read the commandment about drinking from one's own wells figuratively.
comments.comment: For he did not observe that the righteous do not build cisterns but dig “wells” (Genesis 26:18–22), seeking to find the spring that lies within and the source of good things fit to drink, since they also take in a figurative sense the commandment that says: “Drink waters from your own vessels and from the spring of your own wells. Let not your waters overflow outside your own spring, but let your waters pass through into your streets. Let them be yours alone, and let no stranger share them with you” (Proverbs 5:15–17).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The verse shows abundance and also no one sharing the enjoyment.
comments.comment: See how it shows not only ease through abundance, but also having no one a partner in enjoyment; and it doubles itself and calls it possession; for one knows the pleasure of the matter.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wife of one's youth is the knowledge of God, given to us from the beginning, which is also called mother and sister.
comments.comment:
Let your spring of water be your own, and rejoice with the wife of your youth (Proverbs 5:18). If the woman here signifies the knowledge of God, this was given to us from youth; thus the knowledge of God was given to us from the beginning, for which Solomon speaks of a more profound teaching in youth: 'For son, let not a bad counsel seize you' (Proverbs 2:17)—saying the devil, as one who counsels wickedly—'leaving behind the teaching of youth and a divine testament.' But forgetfulness and the loss of knowledge and possession are second evils, just as extreme sickness is second to health and death is second to life.

It is also to be understood at once that the same knowledge is called both mother and wife and sister. Mother, because he who taught me through her has brought me into being, as Paul did through the gospel in Galatians. Wife, because, being with me, she brings forth virtues and correct doctrines, … And sister, because both I and you have come from the one God and Father: 'for I have said,' he says, 'that your wisdom is to be your sister.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the wife of youth is and why the verse is worded so.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Friendship and grace are virtue and knowledge, and to be 'many' is to possess many contemplations.
comments.comment: Let the deer of friendship and the foal of your graces converse with you; and let your own wisdom be esteemed by you and be understood by you at all times; for by behaving in this friendship, one will be many. If 'grace and friendship set free,' but virtue and knowledge set free a rational soul, then grace and friendship are virtue and knowledge. If the deer is born of friendship, and the foal is born of grace, the deer is a symbol of contemplation, and the foal of apatheia; for the one is destined to come from virtues, and the other from knowledge. Virtue and the knowledge of God are proper to the rational nature. To be 'many' is to possess a multitude of contemplations. And a multitude is that which is beneficial.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Some take being 'not much' toward the stranger as a warning against outside wisdom, others against lingering in evil thoughts.
comments.comment: Regarding 'Be not much toward strangeness' (Proverbs 5:20), some think it is said concerning external wisdom, for which it is not necessary to spend time because of the hidden deceits; others will take it concerning evil, and will interpret being 'not much' toward it as follows: that it is not possible for a man, being a man, to entirely abstain from evil thoughts, but it is possible not to linger in them; and that he calls 'stranger's embraces' the evil thoughts which seize the soul and do not escape the God who knows the heart.
comments.selected_reason: Gives two plain readings of the warning against the stranger.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Whoever guarantees Christ gives his own soul to enemies who war against those friendly to the Savior.
comments.comment: Son, if you have a friend near you, will you give your hand to an enemy? Everyone who guarantees Christ, the friend of the apostles, as righteousness and truth, gives his own soul to those enemies who are accustomed to war against men because of their friendship toward the Savior; for friendship is the spiritual knowledge of God, by which also the holy friends become rich in God. In this way also John the Baptist was a friend of the Bridegroom, and Moses, and the apostles: 'for you do not call me slaves anymore,' he says.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Sleep is sin in action and drowsiness the first unclean thought, and the Law forbids the one, the Gospel the other.
comments.comment: Do not give sleep to your eyes, nor let a watchman stand over your eyelids. Sleep is sin in its activity; but drowsiness is the first unclean thought established in the soul. Therefore also before drowsiness, the Law prevents sleep: 'For it was said,' he says, 'to the ancients: You shall not murder' (Ex 20:13); but I say: You shall not be angry. And here, for it seems to me, the Law prevents sleep, but the Gospel of Christ prevents drowsiness, if indeed the one cuts off sin in its activity, while the other cuts off the evil first established according to the intellect.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the warning against sleep in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The ant, with no one to compel it, prepares its food, and the verse calls this natural movement wisdom.
comments.comment: Go to the ant, O sluggard, and observe its ways and become wiser than it (Prov 6:6); for even without a farmer being there, and not having one to compel him, and not being under a master, it prepares its food for the summer. Note here that it calls the natural and harmonious movement of the ant wisdom; …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the ant is called wise.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Perhaps God gave irrational creatures an imitation of reason, so that looking at ants rational beings become more industrious.
comments.comment: We must rather marvel at the divine nature, which has extended even to irrational creatures something like an imitation of rational beings, perhaps to put rational beings to shame: so that, looking at ants, they may become more industrious and more careful to store up what is useful to them (Proverbs 6:6–8) …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the ant is held up to the sluggard.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The ant is free of the slavery to God that belongs to virtue and knowledge, yet has God as Creator.
comments.comment: And how could it not be under a master, if all things are slaves of God? Or is God ever called a master in two ways, as Creator and as known? Therefore also Paul writes: 'But now, having been freed from sin, having become slaves to God' (Rom 6:22), clearly according to virtue and knowledge, 'have your fruit unto sanctification, the end being eternal life.' And if the ant is unworthy of such an end, being irrational, it clearly is also free from such a slavery; so it is well said that the ant is not under a master according to this type of mastery, but is again under a master as having God as Creator.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The sleep meant is wickedness and ignorance, poverty is a lack of knowledge, and want a scarcity of virtues.
comments.comment: Until when, sluggard, will you lie down? When will you arise from sleep? This sleep only happens to a rational soul; for here it signifies wickedness and ignorance, … Poverty happens to you like an evil traveler, and want like a good runner. Poverty is a deprivation of knowledge; and want is a scarcity of virtues.
comments.selected_reason: Says in plain terms what the sleeper's sleep and poverty stand for.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The fool has lost theory; the lawless, practice.
comments.comment: The fool is the atheist who has lost the theoretical, but the lawless one is he who has lost the practical.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Bodily signs like these may let opponents recognize their own thoughts nourished in us, since only God knows hearts.
comments.comment: He himself blows with the eye, but it signifies the foot, and he teaches by blowing with the fingers. Beware here, lest the opponents, through such movements of the body, recognize their own thoughts being nourished in us, since we have believed only God to be the Knower of Hearts.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Whoever eats the flesh of Christ and drinks his blood acquires righteous blood, and without it the soul dies.
comments.comment: An eye of insolence, an unjust tongue, hands pouring out righteous blood. Everyone who eats the flesh of Christ and drinks his blood acquires righteous blood, the deprivation of which is said to cause a rational soul to die; 'for the soul, he says, that sins shall die' (Ezek 18:4).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A false witness divides brothers in Christ, and 'kindles' because passionate thoughts ignite anger, hatred and desire.
comments.comment:
A false witness kindles lies and sends judgments among brothers. Brothers are those having the gift of adoption and being under the same father, Christ, whom the witness of injustice attempts to divide, casting tribulations and judgments among them.

And 'kindles', I think, is placed because of the passionate thoughts igniting the mind toward anger and hatred, and desire toward shameful works. These thoughts the holy Paul also named the fiery arrows of the evil one, piercing the soul and working death (Ephesians 6:16).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The mother is wisdom, who bore us according to God, and through her the son comes to see the father.
comments.comment: 'Guard, son, the laws of your father and do not reject the statutes of your mother...' (Proverbs 6:20-22). Whenever you walk, lead her, and let her be with you. The mother is proposed to be led, who is the wisdom having begotten us according to God. Yet it was necessary for him to say the father; for he is more suitable for being in union with the son. But since it is not possible for him to know God before the contemplation of things having happened, for this reason he proposes the mother and not the father to be led, so that through the mother the son might see the father; for if she does not himself beget him, he does not see the light, which is the knowledge of him, the God.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The commandment of the law is a lamp and light, the Old Testament perhaps being the lamp and the New the light.
comments.comment: That the commandment of the law is a lamp and light and way of life, a reproof and instruction. … And perhaps the Old Testament is a lamp: 'for he was the lamp that was burning and shining' (John 5:35); but the New Testament is light: 'for I, he says, am the light of the world' (John 8:12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the lamp and the light of the verse with the two Testaments.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The soul a woman hunts is precious, since it is not earthy by nature.
comments.comment: She hunts. And the soul hunted by a woman is precious by nature, for it is not earthy by nature. Or again: since the mindset and soul of the brave are precious, she still hunts even these.
comments.selected_reason: Explains whose soul the woman hunts, in one plain thought.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The pleasure of wickedness is worth one loaf.
comments.comment: For the honor of a prostitute is as much as one loaf. For such is the pleasure of wickedness as much as one loaf.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The fire in the bosom is an unchaste thought allowed to linger; the coals are sin in action.
comments.comment: Will someone release fire in his bosom and not burn his clothes? Or will someone walk upon coals of fire and burn his feet? This one releases the fire in the bosom, the one forgiving the unchaste thought in the heart, corrupting the righteous thoughts through lingering. And this one walks upon the coals, the one destroying his own soul through the energy of sin.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the fire and the coals stand for.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: No one who goes in to an unchaste woman is acquitted, for the devil is the man of her.
comments.comment:
Thus the one who entered toward an unchaste woman will not be acquitted, nor everyone touching her. An unchaste woman speaks of wickedness; for the devil is the man of her, who begets with her the lawless sons.

And the Savior says in the Gospels to the Jews: 'You are of your father the devil' (John 8:44).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A thief steals to fill a hungry soul, and when caught by true knowledge he lays aside all false knowledge.
comments.comment: It is no wonder if someone catches a thief; for he steals in order to fill a hungry soul. If he is caught, he will pay sevenfold and, by giving all his possessions, he will save himself. But if he is caught by true knowledge, he will lay aside all false knowledge, he who formerly stole through the need of knowledge from the foolishness made mad by our Savior's wisdom.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Everyone who shares in the adulteress's evil shares in the devil, the first to rejoice in evil.
comments.comment: And the adulteress, through the need of wits, procures destruction for her soul. Everyone who has shared in the evil of the adulteress is a partaker of the devil, the first who rejoiced in evil and who from the beginning has been a murderer.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: In the day of judgment we will have the devil as our accuser.
comments.comment: For the mind of a man full of zeal for it will show no mercy in the day of judgment. There he shows that we will have the devil as an accuser of the things done to us in the day of judgment. And this also the holy Paul says: 'so that the one against us, having nothing to say, may appear nothing trivial concerning us' (Titus 2:8).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Keeping the divine commandments shines for us more brightly than the light of the eyes.
comments.comment: Guard the common, so that it may be yours, he says, and to live an eternal life, and to become discerning. For the keeping of the divine commandments will shine for us much more brightly than the light of the eyes.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The hand is the whole action and the finger the partial.
comments.comment: The hand is the whole action, but the finger is the more partial. Convinced, he says, you will have a wide heart for the reception of the virtues.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Wisdom is our sister because the Father who made the incorporeal nature made this too, and here wisdom means the contemplation of created things.
comments.comment: I have said that your wisdom is a sister; make practical understanding known to yourself. Our sister is wisdom, because he who made the incorporeal nature is Father and has made this. And there he speaks of wisdom not as the Son of God, but as the contemplation of bodies and incorporeal things, and of the judgment and providence in them, the vision of which is understanding, and knowledge, and instruction, and discernment.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why wisdom is called a sister.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Words that strike with charm are passions of thought.
comments.comment: In order that he may keep you from an alien and evil woman, if she should strike you with words of charm. The words that strike with charm are passions of thought.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The window is the flesh of the man, through which the evil one works his snares for those who wish it.
comments.comment: For peeping from a window of her house into the streets, seeing the youth of any of the foolish children, lacking in wits, passing by a corner in the passages of her house, and speaking in the evening darkness, whenever the nocturnal silence is thick, the woman meets him having a prostitute-like appearance, which causes the hearts of the young to fall away. He now calls the flesh of the man a window; for through this the evil one works his snares for those who wish to do so.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Vice does not at first force a man onto the broad road, but meets him at once if he gives himself over to pleasures.
comments.comment: But here, one must attend to what Solomon says concerning vice: that it does not lead a man initially onto the broad road, nor does it force him to walk through the passages of its house, or approach a corner, or speak in the evening darkness; rather, if he sees someone giving himself over to pleasures, there immediately 'an appearance having met him, it is a fornication, which causes the hearts of the young to wander' (Proverbs 7:10).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: An unclean thought is a mental corner, so vice sitting at every corner deceives the soul through all unclean thoughts.
comments.comment: … of the thoughts some are pure and others are unclean—and if of lines the straight ones are called straight, but the bent ones are not straight, a corner being a bent straight line—then an unclean thought is a mental corner. Therefore, vice sitting by every corner signifies its deceiving the soul through all the unclean thoughts. And a demonic passion is an impression moved toward shameful work, calling out the soul.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Vice seeks to disgrace the face of our soul through curtains, bed, cushions, saffron and cinnamon, which are various evil passions.
comments.comment: 'Because of this I went out to meet you; longing for your face, I have found you' (Prov 7:15); … 'I have spread my bed with curtains; I have made my couch with cushions of Egypt' (Prov 7:16); … 'I have torn my veil with saffron; my house with cinnamon' (Prov 7:17). Vice seeks to disgrace the face of our soul through the curtains, the bed, the cushions, the saffron, and the cinnamon, which are various evil passions as they occur according to the inventors of evils.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Almost every practical sin begins in the word, as the young man is ensnared by the prostitute's enticing speech.
comments.comment: For almost every practical sin has its beginning in the word. Regarding the young man whom the prostitute—who is personified in the proverbs, that is, being a woman or a false glory or a deception starting from words—is able to ensnare: for it is said, 'She led him astray with much intercourse' or enticement, and 'with the nooses through the lips she hollowed him out' (Proverbs 7:21/7). … And behold, the word has become the beginning of sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the young man in the verse is led astray.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Countless' does not mean infinite, but too worthless to be numbered.
comments.comment: Regarding the prostitute, it is indeed said: 'They are countless, whom you have slain' (Proverbs 7:26). This does not necessarily mean that they are infinite, but that they are not worthy of being numbered. They do not exist in any word or number.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'countless' means in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those persuaded become earthly and mortal and so perish.
comments.comment: The ways of Hades, leading down into the chambers of death. For those who are persuaded by it, becoming earthly and mortal through it, thus they shall perish.
comments.selected_reason: Short and clear on the end of the woman's house.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Wisdom is praised at exits and entrances, beside those coming out of evil and entering into virtue.
comments.comment: For it is upon the high edges; and in the midst of the soft ones, courage stands between recklessness and cowardice. For it lies in wait by the gates of the powerful; and in the entrances it is praised. Wisdom is said to be praised sometimes in exits and sometimes in entrances, that is, beside those coming out from evil and entering into virtue; for he names the one coming out and the one entering as exit and entrance. Often we have noted this habit of his, that from the states he names those who possess the states, that is, the best ones or the worst ones.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Virtue is spoken of as that which accompanies the heart.
comments.comment: Perceive, you who are without malice, the craftiness; but you who are uneducated, put a heart within you. Here, Cardia has spoken of virtue as that which accompanies the heart.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Instruction and knowledge are contained within wisdom, which is first the gift of the Holy Spirit.
comments.comment: Take instruction and not silver, and knowledge instead of tested gold... For wisdom is better than precious stones. There, Wisdom took as a genus the instruction and the knowledge; for having placed instruction and knowledge before, she leads into it; 'for wisdom is better than precious stones' (Proverbs 8:11), as instruction and knowledge are contained within wisdom, which is first the gift of the Holy Spirit, if indeed 'a word of wisdom is given through the Spirit' (1 Corinthians 2:13). And this same thing is also called the spirit of adoption (Romans 8:15).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The fear of the Lord hates injustice, insolence and the ways of the wicked, so no one who has it acts unjustly.
comments.comment: No one having the divine fear before his eyes sins; for the divine fear is a refuter of sin. When men despise it, sinning occurs, having become outside of the divine fear. In the same way also the divine writing of the proverbs introduces wisdom, saying: 'The fear of the Lord hates injustice, and insolence and pride and the ways of the wicked' (Prov 8:13). If the fear of God hates these things, no one having it acts unjustly; for 'the fear of the Lord hates injustice.' He is not an insolent man, he is not a slanderer, he is not self-willed. And the name of insolence (hybris) at times signifies slander, and at other times exaltation and arrogance. 'And the ways of the wicked the fear of God hates.' And the 'ways of the wicked' are the ungodly opinions and the lawless actions.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the fear of the Lord hates and why it keeps from sin.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Injustice, insolence and pride are named for the unrighteous, the insolent and the proud.
comments.comment: The fear of the Lord hates injustice, and insolence and pride, and the ways of the wicked (Proverbs 8:13). Note that he speaks of injustice and insolence and pride regarding the unrighteous, the insolent, and the proud, from the worst ways.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Said of the divinity, 'he created me' means 'he appointed me' as the beginning of his providential and creative works.
comments.comment: "The Lord created me" (Proverbs 8:22). If you take "he created me" as referring to the divinity, it means "he appointed me." So too: "Create a clean heart in me, O God" (Psalm 50:12 LXX; Psalm 51:10 in modern Hebrew numbering). And: "that he might create the two in himself" (Ephesians 2:15). For it is not in essence that he might create those who had already come into being, but that he might appoint them. Therefore he appointed me as the beginning of his providential and creative works. And to David he says: "I was appointed king by him."
comments.selected_reason: Explains the word 'created' in the verse in simple terms.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The wisdom begotten from God was created among men in Christ, the beginning of his ways, to give us the way back through humility.
comments.comment: But since the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), that same wisdom begotten from God deigned also to be created among human beings. This is what the text means: “The Lord created me in the beginning of his ways” (Proverbs 8:22). For the beginning of his ways is the head of the church, which is Christ clothed with humanity, through whom an example of living was given to us—that is, the sure way by which we might reach God. We could not return except through humility, since we fell through pride, as was said to our first creation: “Taste, and you will be like gods” (Genesis 3:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse as speaking of Christ's coming among us, with a reason a reader can follow.
comments.author: Augustine of Hippo

comments.capsule: He said 'created' not 'begat', since creating belongs to a lord, begetting to a father.
comments.comment: … even if the Savior says: 'the Lord created me' (Proverbs 8:22), he says it at the right time; for he did not say: 'the Lord begat me'; for to beget belongs to a father, but to create belongs to a lord.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Wisdom exists before creation, and is called principle only through its relation to created things.
comments.comment: Signifying many things, as we have said, the principle now denotes the eternal, and the cause, and the productive. And the principle of some things is a principle, and signifies a relation, but not subsistence. For things toward something are such: as the right and the left. Therefore, the Wisdom of God, being a subsistence, is not a principle of any things; for before creation, Wisdom exists. But when it receives a relation toward created things, then it becomes a principle of the productive and providential ways of God, toward the works which have their existence from the Creator, having contributed nothing to it toward being Wisdom; but the relation through which it is called principle and creator, that came to be when the created things came to be. For a principle does not pre-exist those of which it is a principle; nor are these said to exist with it, if the creatures possess their subsistence in time. For Wisdom, being eternal, is not subject to time.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Called 'created', the pre-existing Wisdom has a relation to creatures, and the Son is said to be created because he was born of Mary, to be our teacher.
comments.comment: Therefore the principle is a spouse to the creatures. The Son of God, pre-existing the creation, being Wisdom, if he says, 'The Lord created me,' he does not have the thought of subsistence, but rather a relation toward the creatures. For he says he is created for works, being the principle of the productive and providential ways of God, that is to say, the cause, to speak more introductory. The Son of God has become man, taking the form of a slave; and being from before the ages and eternal, in that which God is the Word, he is said to be created because he had birth from Mary, becoming flesh; so that those who wish to walk according to God and toward God may use a teacher, providing a pattern of excellent life and instruction to those who follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Created' does not always mean coming into being, as in David's prayer for a clean heart and Paul's one new man.
comments.comment: That 'created' does not always signify subsistence, is shown by David saying, 'Create in me a clean heart, O God' (Psalm 51:10). For he asks not as one not possessing, to receive, but as one having cast it away, to receive it again having been cleansed. And Paul, saying the two are created into one new man (Ephesians 2:15), does not signify the subsistence of men, but a union from concord; just as those who interpreted 'He created me' brought it forth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Insofar as he is Wisdom, he is the beginning.
comments.comment: For insofar as he is firstborn of all creation, he is first; and insofar as he is Wisdom, he is beginning. For so says Wisdom through Solomon, that "The Lord created me a beginning of his ways." (Proverbs 8:22)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The words 'The Lord created me' are said about the Church, which is being created in him.
comments.comment: In the same way, when he says, "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways" (Proverbs 8:22), he says this about the Church, which is being created in him. For the maker of all things is not a creature or a thing made; rather, the thing made is being renewed in the maker, as Paul says: "We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus" (Ephesians 2:10).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'The Lord created me' as said of the Church, created anew in Christ.
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
comments.work: On the Incarnation and against the Arians

comments.capsule: 'Founded' refers to the economy predestined according to his flesh, the one foundation being Jesus Christ.
comments.comment: 'Before the age he founded me,' calling this a foundation, refers to the economy predestined according to his flesh. … As also the apostle says, 'for no one can lay another foundation except that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ' (1 Corinthians 3:11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'founded before the age' means, with a Bible parallel.
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra

comments.capsule: The earth is our flesh needing healing, and the abysses are the saints' hearts.
comments.comment: Then he says, 'in the beginning,' 'before making the earth' (Proverbs 8:23). What earth, this one? Meaning our flesh, the earth which becomes again after the disobedience. … For 'earth' he says, 'I am,' and 'and into earth I shall depart' (Genesis 3:19). For it was necessary for this to receive healing, having shared in some way with the Holy Word. … Then he says, 'before making the abysses' (Proverbs 8:24); here the prophet proverbially says the abysses are the hearts of the saints, those having the gift of the Spirit in their own depth.
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra

comments.capsule: The springs are the apostles, and the mountains and hills are the apostles and their successors.
comments.comment: Regarding the number of the apostles, twelve springs are remembered. Thus, concerning the fleshly generation, the Lord spoke through the prophet Solomon, saying, 'before the springs of the waters came forth' (Proverbs 8:24). Likewise, the Savior said toward the holy springs, 'having gone, make disciples of all nations' (Matt 28:19). It is evident from everywhere that the holy apostles and springs were tropically named by the prophet. Since we have spoken about those that went before, it follows to fill up the remainder. The remainder concerns the mountains and the hills. For he says, 'before the mountain was established' (Proverbs 8:25), and 'before all the hills, I beget you' (Proverbs 8:25). He calls the apostles and the successors of the apostles mountains and hills, so that the just administration concerning them might be indicated proverbially among other men.
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra

comments.capsule: 'Before all the hills he begets me' is spoken in the person of the Church, created first and afterward begotten.
comments.comment: And when he says, "Before all the hills he begets me" (Proverbs 8:25), he speaks from the person of the Church, which was created first and afterward is begotten from God. This is why in Proverbs the words "The Lord created me" (Proverbs 8:22) come first, and "he begot me" comes later.
