comments.selected_reason: Explains why the passage says 'created' first and 'begets' later.
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
comments.work: On the Incarnation and against the Arians

comments.capsule: Because God could not be conceived apart from the Word, the Word, who was in the Father before the world, came forth as its maker.
comments.comment:
Since it was impossible to conceive of God apart from the Word and the wisdom approaching the Word regarding the construction of the heavens, he rightly said, 'Whenever he was preparing the heavens, I was with him' (Proverbs 8:27).

For before the world existed, the Word was in the Father. When the Almighty God set to make all things in the heavens and upon the earth, the genesis of the world required an active energy. And because of this, with no other existing besides God (for all is confessed to have come from him), the Word, having come forth, became the maker of the world, he who previously was inwardly preparing it, just as the prophet Solomon teaches us, saying, 'Whenever he was preparing the heavens, I was with him' (Proverbs 8:27) …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse as the Word's part in making the heavens.
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra

comments.capsule: The Son, the Father's will and Wisdom, was co-partner in preparing the heavens.
comments.comment: And the Son is the will of Him, through whom all things consist, being the Wisdom of the One Begetting, saying: 'Whenever I was preparing the heavens, I was co-partner with Him' (Proverbs 8:27).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'I was', said of God, marks no time, so Wisdom who was with God is everlasting.
comments.comment: “I was the one in whom he rejoiced.” Said of God, “I was” does not mark time. It is temporal when it points to something under time, as in “I was in the marketplace.” But if she was with God in a way that fits the One without beginning, she herself is everlasting.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says 'I was' of Wisdom.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The house that Wisdom built for herself is Jesus, born of Mary, and each believer is likewise raised up as a temple of God.
comments.comment: According to another understanding, [in Zechariah] the house being rebuilt in Jerusalem, which is Jesus, who was brought forth from Mary, having been built by the wisdom of God, has according to the proverbial decree thus: 'Wisdom built a house for herself' (Proverbs 9:1), concerning which the building wisdom said to the opponents: 'Destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it up' (John 2:19); this, he says, 'was speaking about the temple of his body,' as the evangelist wrote. Regarding the things said, each of the faithful is also a house being raised up to be a temple of God. 'For do you not know, he says, that you are a temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you?' (1 Corinthians 3:16).
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly who the house of Wisdom is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Wisdom lays a table of wise teachings and mixes her wine, joining the Word with the Incarnation, giving each person what he can contain.
comments.comment:
She has laid upon it [the table] 'having slaughtered her own victims' (Prov 9:2). And she has laid upon it 'her own wine' (Proverbs 9:2), 'mixing' it with this table, and she calls all to eat and drink from this table. And we call here the table of wisdom the divine one for children. And sacrifices are laid upon this; for when we perform the sacred rites and slaughter the doctrines of piety, so that we may make them ready for food, then the sacrifices are laid upon the table. And no one else offered them except Wisdom herself, who 'prepared her own table' (Prov 9:2); for she did not simply say, 'she prepared a table,' but 'her own.' And the table of Wisdom does not have other delicacies laid upon it except the wise teachings.

Furthermore, she 'mixed her own wine' (Proverbs 9:2). She took water to it, so that we, being unable to receive it unmixed, might take wine already mixed. There are certain unspeakable words, which are not let to be called wine. When anyone is able to lead these into explicit teaching, she mixed, adding to them a perceptible gift: the examples of the Scripture, the words announced in parables. Again, since God is the Word and Wisdom is the Word, but we were not able to take the Word unmixed, she mixed it with the Incarnation, and we received, moreover, mixed wine from both the Word of the Incarnation and the majesty of the Only-begotten. 'And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory' (John 1:14). Behold the mixture. This was not the mixing of anyone else but of her own Wisdom. You know that the one mixing sometimes makes the mixture according to the capacity of the drinker. And so Wisdom mixed her own wine and does not give the same mixture to all, but what each can contain.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Wisdom's table and mixed wine are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christians teach everyone with the word of God, even the foolish, as Wisdom herself invites those who lack sense to eat her bread and drink her wine.
comments.comment: We admit that we want to educate everyone with the word of God, even if Celsus does not wish it, so as to give adolescents too the encouragement that suits them, and to show house-slaves how, by taking on a free spirit, they may be made noble by the word. Those among us who champion Christianity say plainly enough that they are debtors “to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish” (Romans 1:14). For they do not deny that they must heal the souls of the foolish too, so that, as far as possible, they may lay aside their ignorance and hasten toward greater understanding. They hear Solomon also when he says, “And you who are foolish, apply your heart” (Proverbs 8:5), and, “Whoever of you is most foolish, let him turn aside to me; and to those who lack sense I, Wisdom, give this charge, saying: Come, eat my bread, and drink the wine I have mixed for you; forsake folly, that you may live, and set your understanding straight in knowledge” (Proverbs 9:4–6).
comments.selected_reason: Shows whom Wisdom's invitation is for.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Rebuke is to be given to be useful and at the right time, since a wise man loves the one who rebukes him and a wicked man hates it.
comments.comment: 'Do not rebuke evildoers, so that they may not hate you' (Proverbs 9:8). The word teaches not to avoid being hated by the wicked, but says this: rebuke, so that you may be useful. Approaching to rebuke not at the right time—for 'there is a rebuke that is not beautiful'—does not benefit the one being rebuked, but rather makes him even more wicked, as to hate the one rebuking. 'Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you' (Proverbs 9:8). If the wise man being rebuked loves the one bringing the rebuke, it is clear that the one who hates the rebuke is wicked.
comments.selected_reason: Explains when and to whom rebuke is useful.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A rebuke can be given by word, showing the one in error his fault.
comments.comment: And often there is rebuke when the one in whom the error is, is shown by word to the responsible party; for it says: 'Rebuke the wise, and he will love you' (Prov 9:8). The wise man rebukes the lesser wise man, the one being led in.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Fear and shame are called teachers because they stand for the teaching that turns us from wickedness and leads us to a sense of our sins.
comments.comment: A foolish and impudent woman becomes lacking in shame, one who does not know shame; since shame is a teacher, it is said 'she does not know shame.' And David says that the fear of God is a teacher: 'Come, children, listen to me, I will teach you the fear of the Lord' (Psalm 34:11). But if fear and shame are natural passions of the soul, how are they teachers? Perhaps he calls the teaching about the fear of the Lord 'the fear of the Lord,' which teaches us that we must turn away from wickedness, as it is said, 'all shall turn from evil by the fear of the Lord' (Proverbs 16:6). Again, he calls 'shame' the discourses concerning repentance and shame that lead us to a sense of our own sins.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Lawless treasures do not profit, but righteousness rescues from death, so it is righteousness that is to be treasured, as wealth kept in heaven.
comments.comment: And often what one has treasured, he leaves behind. Sometimes, as a year passes, he falls away into other things. Therefore, it is not necessary to be anxious about treasuring in this way; for 'lawless treasures will not profit, but righteousness rescues from death' (Proverbs 10:2). Therefore, the righteousness that rescues from death and from every other evil is to be treasured. This wealth is treasured in heaven.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what is worth treasuring.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The soul that opens its eyes to the bread of the divine word is not starved.
comments.comment: The one having opened the eyes of the soul and having been filled by the manner of chewing the bread of the divine logos does not suffer from famine; for 'the Lord will not let the soul of the righteous starve' (Proverbs 10:3). Whoever is in desire for bread but is not opening his eyes to his own bread, lives in famine; for the soul has many foods from God within itself.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the Lord will not let the righteous soul starve.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wise son saved from the heat is the one who escapes the heat of sin, though the righteous man still feels the heat of the senses.
comments.comment: And the servant who serves God intellectually is there, obtaining shade and rest, having escaped the heat of life: 'a wise son was saved from the heat' (Proverbs 10:5), not being consumed by the heat, according to those in the parable who did not receive the seed into depth and fell by the flame of sin. This promise is said to David in the Psalms: 'the sun shall not strike you by day, nor the moon by night' (Ps 121:6), which according to the literal sense we do not find. For he himself, being righteous, was labored upon by the heat of the sensible, but was unlabored upon by the heat of sin.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The rod is the rebuke and corrective word, which instructs rather than harms, so that sparing it would be hatred rather than love.
comments.comment: For this rebuke and all that is from God does not harm the one being rebuked, but instructs him. And that it is thus, Paul writes to the Corinthians: "What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love?" (1 Cor 4:21), which is to say: Shall I approach as a beloved, or as required for correction? For a certain way of the one being corrected by oppressors seems to suggest that he does not love him. A wise saying has also been said regarding the rod: "For he who brings wisdom from his lips strikes a heartless man with a rod" (Proverbs 10:13), calling the rebuke and the corrective word a rod. Since this is useful, the divine word presents it, saying: "He who spares his rod hates his own son" (Prov 13:24), even though according to men, one might be thought to love by not striking the son.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the rod means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Silver stands for the divine word, and the tongue of the righteous is silver because the tongue signifies the word.
comments.comment: Often, the divine teachings and the word are signified by this name: 'The words of the Lord are pure words, like silver refined in a furnace, tested, cleansed in the earth seven times' (Ps 12:6). And again, it is said proverbially: 'The tongue of the righteous is like refined silver' (Prov 10:20). For the word is signified by the name of the tongue.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the image of the tongue as silver.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The tongue of the righteous is called silver because the tongue is the instrument of the word, refined by sharing in the heavenly light.
comments.comment: For just as silver signifies the word, it is clear from 'the tongue of the righteous, refined silver' (Proverbs 10:20). It is not because of sensible silver, but since the tongue is an instrument of the word, it has taken this as a symbol. This has been refined not concerning chance matters, but by partaking of the heavenly light, which Jesus came to earth to cast, desiring it already to be revealed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Ungodly hopes end in destruction.
comments.comment: The ungodly have only evil hopes; for everything they hope for is destruction (Proverbs 10:28).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A righteous man who dies finds what he hoped for.
comments.comment: When a righteous man dies, he does not regret (Proverbs 11:7); for if the righteous man dies, he finds the things he expected and did not regret having labored for them.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly why the righteous do not regret death.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Trust in wealth ends in a fall, as Lazarus and the rich man show.
comments.comment: … For 'he who has trusted in wealth will fall, but he who grasps what is just will rise' (cf. Proverbs 11:28), just as Lazarus was carried into the bosom of Abraham (Luke 16:22), but the rich man is delivered to the torment having fallen upon it (Luke 16:23), who through arrogance overlooked Lazarus.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a Gospel example of the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The tree of life is the one in paradise, kept from Adam after his sin.
comments.comment: A tree of life grows from the fruit of righteousness: This tree of life is the one planted in the midst of paradise, which Adam is prevented from touching after the sin, having cast away the seeds of righteousness, from which the tree of life grows.
comments.selected_reason: Says what the tree of life is.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Those agreeing on evil have no right to take counsel with God, but the pious take counsel with him and do right.
comments.comment: … For it is not right for those who wish to agree together on some evil thing to take counsel with God. But everyone who is pious and good and a lover of righteousness will take counsel with God and will go on to do what must be done. For it is written: “The thoughts of the righteous are judgments” (Proverbs 12:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the thoughts of the righteous are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: When the thoughts of the righteous are sound their words follow, as the good man brings forth good out of the treasure of his heart.
comments.comment: For the law of God is in the heart of the righteous; he meditates on wisdom and his steps are not made to slip, which are "the walking powers of the soul." Such a thing also the saying of Proverbs means, "the judgments of the thoughts of the righteous" (Proverbs 12:5). And when such thoughts exist, the word follows to be like this: "for the good man brings forth good out of the good treasure of the heart" (Luke 6:45).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mind of the holiest saints is holy and full of good thoughts, so it is fitting that it be dedicated to the pure God.
comments.comment: … For the mind of the holiest saints is truly holy, and holy in the highest degree, and so it would be fitting for it to be dedicated to the wholly pure God. For it is full of good thoughts, and it gives off the fragrant ointment of the true knowledge of God; for, as it is written, ‘the thoughts of the righteous are just judgments’ (Proverbs 12:5).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: Some who are not wholly given over to sin still take care to hide their faults, for the wise will hide their own shame.
comments.comment: … For some have not wholly given themselves over to sin. They know, indeed, that at times they are weak and held by the greedy cravings of the flesh, and they do not claim to be clear of other faults either; for ‘we all stumble in many ways’ (James 3:2), as it is written. All the same, they shake off as something ugly any wish to behave shamefully with nothing to cover them, and no one could persuade them to practice their wrongdoing openly and without concealment. They take great care to escape notice; for ‘the wise will hide their own shame’ (Proverbs 12:16), as it is written. This, I think, is what it means to have scales as a kind of covering.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: True goods are the wealth that ransoms a soul, and their lack is ruinous.
comments.comment: … For “the wealth” that consists in true goods “is the ransom of a man’s soul”, according to Solomon, while the poverty opposed to it is ruinous; because of it “the poor man does not stand up to a threat” (Proverbs 13:8).
comments.selected_reason: Says what kind of wealth is a man's ransom.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He who keeps company with the holy takes on their virtue, and he who keeps company with the crooked perverts his own life.
comments.comment: Another will say that these [verses of Psalm 17:26-28] are not spoken toward God but toward a man: that the one spending time with the holy should imitate their virtue, and the one spending time with the wicked should undergo perversion, as the divine writing of Proverbs says: 'He who walks with the wise will be wise, but he who walks with fools will be destroyed' (Prov 13:20). … But he who wishes to be taken toward a man says that the one associating with a holy man becomes holy from the holy things being done, as Elisha with Elijah and Timothy with Paul; and the one hastening with the innocent, having seized that one's virtue, will be innocent. Likewise, the one spending time with an elect man, but the one associating with the crooked, desiring to become like him, will pervert his own life.
comments.selected_reason: Shows how company shapes a person.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteous will consume the wealth of the impious, which is wickedness.
comments.comment: Wealth is stored up for the righteous of those sinning: The wealth of the impious is wickedness. But the righteous will consume it, clearly through good teaching, whether now or even in the age to come, having become more than fifteen cities (Luke 19:17).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Wisdom is an invincible weapon that nothing evil opposes, and against it the demons are powerless.
comments.comment: All things are contrary to a foolish man; but the lips of the wise are weapons of perception. For 'it does not oppose' wisdom 'anything evil,' because it is an invincible weapon; for the demons are only powerless against it.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: 'House' in Scripture means a disposition or way of life, so the houses needing cleansing are base dispositions of the mind and the acceptable ones are virtuous.
comments.comment: And indeed, we find 'house' used by the saints in the divine writings to mean a disposition, a way of life, a virtue, just as it is written concerning the midwives of the Hebrews: "because the midwives feared God, they made houses for themselves" (Exodus 1:21), which shows the virtue constructed by them from the fear of God. For they were not without dwellings before this. And what is said in Proverbs: 'The houses of transgressors will require cleansing, but the houses of the righteous are acceptable' (Proverbs 14:9). For this is said not of sensible things but of the dispositions in the mind — the base ones needing cleansing, the virtuous ones proving acceptable; 'acceptable' meaning not 'choiceworthy to someone' but 'worthy of praise.' For the good is choiceworthy even if no one chooses it, and acceptable even if no one accepts it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'houses' means in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Cleansed, the righteous may see God, the blessed end kept for every rational nature.
comments.comment: The houses of the foolish must undergo cleansing; but the houses of the righteous are receptive, so that having become pure, they may see God; for this is the blessed end which is preserved for all rational nature.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: 'Thoughts' here means the states of the virtues, set against the reckless man's ways.
comments.comment: The reckless man will be filled with his own ways; but a good man is known from his thoughts. Regarding thoughts, he has now spoken of the states of virtues, just as he set them in opposition to the ways of the reckless.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: 'Simple' can mean the guileless, or one who believes every plausible word.
comments.comment: Here 'simple' means the one not having guile, not the well-disposed; for the name signifies both. … the 'simple believes every word' (Proverbs 14:15) signifying the one who is uncontrolled and unable to discern the falsehood in the words, believing everything plausible.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two senses of 'simple'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Perception is set against wickedness, so it signifies virtue.
comments.comment: The foolish are divided by wickedness; but the cunning will prevail through perception. He set wickedness in opposition to perception. If wickedness opposes virtue, then perception now signifies virtue.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Reverence is a stronghold for those establishing holiness and righteousness, yet the one covered by it asks to be guarded by God himself.
comments.comment: In the divine writing of Proverbs, reverence is called a stronghold for those establishing holiness and righteousness, thus: 'A stronghold is the fear of the Lord' (Proverbs 14:26). [Of the psalmist:] He, having been covered by the fear of God, surpassing this covering, wishing to be guarded by God Himself, says to Him through prayer: 'Become for me a protector, a strong place to save me' (Psalm 31:2)
comments.selected_reason: Says what it means that the fear of the Lord is a stronghold.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Strength comes from increasing righteousness, and the ungodly are uprooted.
comments.comment: In increasing righteousness there is much strength; but the ungodly are uprooted from the earth. 'Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will by no means enter the kingdom of heaven' (Matt 5:20).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The lips of the wise are taught by perception, so they open only for what is beneficial and close when what is said would harm.
comments.comment: … 'The lips of the wise are taught by perception' (Proverbs 15:7). When someone speaks having perceived, the lips are taught, not opening them to every word, but to what is beneficial. 'I will open my lips and my mouth shall proclaim your praise' (Ps 51:14). He who has the taught lips, having perceived that what he intends to speak is beneficial, opened them. But when they harm what is being uttered, he closes and binds the lips with perception; he binds the word.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the lips of the wise are taught.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God does not accept a gift made from unjust gain, but a pure gift carries the prayer, for the sacrifice of the ungodly is an abomination and the prayers of the upright are acceptable.
comments.comment: For neither is a good deed to the needy from unjust gains acceptable to God, nor is the one who abstains from injustice praiseworthy if he shares nothing of his own. About those who commit injustice and still try to bring gifts to God it is written: “The sacrifice of the ungodly is an abomination to the Lord” (Proverbs 15:8). … For if you are about to bring an offering to God from injustice and robbery, it is better neither to acquire such a possession nor to bring an offering from it. For a pure gift will carry the prayer, as it is written: “The prayers of the upright are acceptable to him” (Proverbs 15:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why an offering from injustice is rejected.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: God loves those who pursue righteousness, and the righteousness pursued is all virtue.
comments.comment: One must pursue peace; for to pursue it in this way does not mean that one has driven it away. You have this also in the Proverbs: 'those pursuing,' it is said, 'love righteousness' (Proverbs 15:9), meaning that God clearly loves them, that is, those who pursue. The righteousness that is pursued is all virtue.
comments.selected_reason: Says what it is that God loves in the righteous.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Reproof means the commandments, which reprove us when we sin.
comments.comment: The education of the inattentive is known by those passing by; but let those who hate reproof perish shamefully. Regarding reproof, he has now spoken of the commandments; for these reprove us when we are sinning.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Sorrow shows in the face when the conscience rebukes, while the wisdom of man brightens it, as happened to Cain.
comments.comment: Sorrow comes to those who use things in a way that is not required, like the fire of the conscience rebuking and demonstrating, even if evil is still held, the impropriety of the actions being performed, from which the countenance of the soul falls, from which also the bodily features receive their decline. Because it is the countenance of the soul, the saying says: 'The wisdom of man brightens his countenance' (Prov 15:13), and 'We reflect the glory of the Lord with a face unveiled' (2 Cor 3:18), the sign of the sensible face being indicated in 'a heart rejoicing, a cheerful countenance, but in sorrows, a gloomy face' (Prov 15:13), which happened to Cain under the rebuke of the conscience (Gen 4:6-7).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Silence is a refuge from wickedness.
comments.comment: All the time the eyes of the evil receive evil; but the good are at rest always. Silence is a refuge from wickedness.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A person who through simplicity cannot hold the greater doctrines yet thinks rightly is better than the sharper man who does not make plain the word of peace.
comments.comment: And I take what is said with Solomon in the Proverbs to teach that he who, through simplicity, cannot hold the more vigorous and greater doctrines — yet does not think amiss — is better than the readier, sharper man who charges more greatly upon realities but does not make plain the word of the peace and harmony of all. The wording runs thus: 'Better a portion of herbs with friendship and grace than a calf from the stall with hatred.' (Proverbs 15:17) Often, at any rate, we have welcomed a private and simpler feast with a good conscience — entertained by those who could set nothing more before us — rather than loftiness of words raised 'against the knowledge of God,' proclaiming with great plausibility a doctrine foreign to the Father who gave 'the law and the prophets,' the Father of our Lord Jesus.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The ways of life are the practical virtues that lead toward knowledge.
comments.comment: Ways of life are the thoughts of the prudent, so that having turned away from Hades, he may be saved. Regarding ways of life, he speaks of the practical virtues which lead toward knowledge.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Houses stand for the virtues, and the Lord destroys the houses of the proud while keeping safe the life of those who serve God.
comments.comment: And “houses” must be understood in the plural as the abundance of virtue; temperance is a house, courage is a house, meekness and others, … There are against these houses, which the Lord destroys: “For the Lord destroys the houses of the insolent; but he has established a boundary for the widow” (Proverbs 15:25). For he destroys the houses of the proud, as it is said: “Capernaum, until you ascend to heaven, shall you be brought down to Hades” (Matt 11:23), and “the one who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 18:14). “He establishes a boundary for the widow,” which is: the house, the life of those serving God, protected from evils.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the houses and the widow's boundary mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The unrepentant are harsh to themselves.
comments.comment: It is not we who are harsh toward the unrepentant — such are harsh to themselves: 'for he who casts off discipline hates himself.' (Proverbs 15:32)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Through righteous men even enemies become friends, as Paul preached that enemies were reconciled to God.
comments.comment: The ways of righteous men are acceptable to the Lord; and through them, even enemies become friends. This is from Paul preaching: 'Those who were once enemies were reconciled to God through the death of His Son'; however, one must take care whether all enemies become friends through the righteous, so that Christ might also say to all: 'I no longer call you slaves, but friends' (John 15:15).
comments.selected_reason: Says how the righteous make enemies friends.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Christ knows hearts and will judge righteously.
comments.comment: A king's lips are a divination (Proverbs 16:10): Christ is the Knower of Hearts, and he will judge the inhabited world in righteousness.
comments.selected_reason: Says whom the king of the verse stands for.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A throne often means a kingdom or a teaching office, as with 'a throne of authority is prepared with righteousness' and the seat of Moses.
comments.comment: For a throne is often taken to mean a kingdom, even if it is used instead of a teaching office, as is clear from 'The Lord King is established forever' (Psalm 29:10), and again: 'Your throne, O God, is unto the ages of ages' (Ps 45:6), and even more: 'A throne of authority is prepared with righteousness' (Proverbs 16:12). But it is also said to the disciples: 'You also shall sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel' (Matt 19:28). When it is said, 'The scribes sat upon the seat of Moses' (Matthew 23:2), this seat is one of teaching.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The king's throne rests on righteousness because he is a righteous judge.
comments.comment: The strength of the throne of his kingdom is righteousness and judgment, since he, as king, is a righteous judge. This is agreed with what is found in Proverbs: 'By righteousness a throne is prepared' (Prov 16:12).
comments.selected_reason: Says why righteousness establishes the throne.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The angel in charge of punishment is called the wrath of God.
comments.comment: The wrath of a king is a messenger of death (Proverbs 16:14), but a wise man will escape him. The angel who stands regarding matters of punishment is called the wrath of God.
comments.selected_reason: Says what the king's wrath is.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Unless the holy one is free of passion, the wrath is allegorical.
comments.comment: “A king’s wrath is a messenger of death, but a wise man will propitiate him”—if the holy one is free of passion; or else the wrath must be read allegorically.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Knowledge of wisdom is better than gold.
comments.comment: Diseases of wisdom are better than gold (Proverbs 16:16), but diseases of prudence are better than silver. Knowledge of wisdom is better than gold, but knowledge of prudence is better than silver.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Knowledge is called epistemic-knowledge because it knows all things.
comments.comment: The heart of a wise man will understand things from his own mouth (Proverbs 16:23); but he will carry epistemic-knowledge upon his lips. Knowledge said epistemic-knowledge to mean knowing all things.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The crooked man of the proverb is Satan, whose deceit separates the saints, who are joined to one another through knowledge.
comments.comment: A crooked man sends out evils and flashes the spark of deceit (Proverbs 16:28), separating friends. The Word attempts to teach the demons, learning from the devil, to attempt to act against the saints and to test them, separating them from the knowledge which is natural for uniting them to the heavenly powers. Solomon, as I think, revealed this very thing through this proverb, calling Satan a crooked man, flashing the sparks of deceit the evil demons, instead of being taught, and the saints, the friends joining one another through knowledge.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The lap stands for the mind or knowledge, and a deceptive lap signifies ignorance.
comments.comment: Everything comes into the laps of the unrighteous (Proverbs 16:33), but all things just are from the Lord (Proverbs 16:33). It should be noted that he spoke of the hearts of the unrighteous as laps here. I think also that everywhere 'lap' signifies either the mind or knowledge. If it is also a deceptive lap, it will signify ignorance.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The wise servant who has turned from evil becomes a steward of God's mysteries, giving each brother knowledge according to his state, as Joshua divided the land among the tribes.
comments.comment:
Having turned away from evil and having prevailed through virtues, he has mastered foolish demons. And such a person will become also a steward of the mysteries of God, giving spiritual knowledge to each of the brothers according to the analogy of their state, sometimes watering the Corinthian with milk, sometimes feeding the Ephesian with firmer food, discussing height and length and breadth and depth, and through these dimensions signifying the division of the logical nature, which contains the discourses concerning the judgment and providence of God, being most profound and fleeing the human condition.

Just so Jesus son of Nun distributed the land of promise to the twelve tribes, which is a symbol of the knowledge of God and of those things having come from Him. … However, it must be known that the discourses concerning the incarnation of Christ and His appearance in Judah are held in reserve for knowledge; for in this lot Christ is born.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The wicked man takes thoughts from the lawless and acts on them, while the righteous man refuses to feed such thoughts within himself.
comments.comment: An evil man obeys the tongue of the lawless; but a righteous man does not give heed to lying lips. This one obeys the tongues of the lawless, he who receives from them thoughts and hastens to act according to them, whereas the righteous is said not to give heed, that is, not to nourish them any further within himself.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'giving heed' to false lips means in plain terms.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Solomon says one who rejoices at another's ruin is not acquitted, yet wisdom may rejoice in a loss that saves, as with the tax collector and the thief.
comments.comment: Indeed, I too shall laugh at your ruin; and I shall rejoice whenever destruction comes to you. How then does Solomon say before the event: “But he who rejoices at the destruction of another shall not be acquitted” (Proverbs 17:5)? Or perhaps wisdom rejoices in this way, just as she rejoiced at the loss of Matthew the tax collector and at the loss of the thief who believed in Christ. For wisdom lost the thief, but lost the tax collector.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Faithful lips do not suit fools, nor false lips the righteous.
comments.comment: Faithful lips do not suit a fool, nor false lips a righteous man: 'For what fellowship has righteousness with lawlessness, or what communion light with darkness?' (2 Cor 6:14).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: We hide wrongs by their opposite virtues, as righteousness hides injustice, and so seek spiritual friendship.
comments.comment: He who hides wrongdoings seeks friendship; but he who hates hiding distinguishes friends and kinsmen. Through righteousness we hide injustice, through self-control we hide intemperance, again through love we hide hatred, and through freedom from greed we hide avarice. We also hide pride through humility and boldness through meekness, seeking the spiritual friendship, which signifies holy knowledge. And according to Paul, some of the saints are said to have become fellow-citizens and kinsmen of Jerusalem, … 'having been built up on the foundation of the apostles and prophets' (Eph 2:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how one 'hides' a wrong: by putting the opposite virtue in its place.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Repaying evil for good is worse than repaying evil for evil, and Israel in the wilderness did it toward God.
comments.comment: He who gives evil instead of good, evil shall not move out from his house. If he who gives evil instead of evil is lawless, how much more the one who gives evil instead of good is more lawless? Such became toward God the Israel of the wilderness, to whom Moses says in Deuteronomy: 'These generations are crooked and perverse, repaying the Lord' (Deut 32:5).
comments.selected_reason: Shows what the verse means with a clear example.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A fool cannot buy wisdom with money because he has no heart for it.
comments.comment: Why did money exist for a fool? For he will not be able to acquire wisdom without a heart. Money belongs to a fool; for regarding each of his matters, there is foolishness; because of these things, having become without a heart, he is unable to acquire wisdom.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why money is no use to a fool in getting wisdom.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Angels and holy men are brothers through adoption in the Spirit, born of Wisdom to lead men from wickedness to virtue.
comments.comment: [Commenting on the proverb 'brothers are useful in necessities':] If the sons of Christ are brothers to one another, and the angels and the righteous men are sons of Christ, then the angels and the holy men are brothers to one another, being born to this through the adoption in the Spirit. For this reason they are born by Wisdom, so that they might lead men from wickedness to virtue and from ignorance to the knowledge of God, if indeed 'the whole creation groans and suffers together and was made subject to futility not by its own will' (Romans 8:22).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Brothers are to be useful in times of need, meaning matters of great importance and pressing urgency.
comments.comment: Andrew [Peter's brother], who fulfilled the command that Solomon wrote long before in Proverbs: 'Let brothers be useful in times of need' (Proverbs 17:17), that is, in matters of great benefit, of great importance, of pressing urgency; for these are what wisdom called needs, as necessary and unavoidable occasions.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'needs' means in the proverb.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: The proud man who exalts his house falls into evils, because the Lord opposes the proud.
comments.comment: He who makes his own house lofty seeks destruction; but he who turns aside from learning will fall into evils. 'He who turns aside from learning,' because 'the Lord opposes the proud' (Proverbs 3:34), 'will fall into evils' (Proverbs 17:20)
comments.selected_reason: Ties the verse to the proverb that God opposes the proud.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Whoever changes readily turns from virtue to wickedness.
comments.comment: A man prone to change will fall into evils; he is one who is prone to change readily from virtue into wickedness.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: One who unjustly takes gifts into his heart has crooked paths, for passionate thoughts are the gifts the demons offer us.
comments.comment: One receiving gifts in his heart unjustly, his paths will not be straight; but the impious one turns away from the paths of righteousness. One receiving unjust thoughts in his heart, his paths will not be straight; for the passionate thoughts are called gifts being offered to us by the demons. Or the impious one will receive gifts in his heart to turn away from the paths of judgment.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'gifts' taken into the heart are.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The wise son has both a father and a mother, but the foolish son has only the one who gave birth to him.
comments.comment: A foolish son is anger to his father and grief to the one who gave birth to him. The wise son has both a father and a mother, but the foolish son has only the one who gave birth to him; for the mother is also the one who gave birth, but the one who gave birth is not always a mother. For if that which was born dies in wickedness and ignorance, she is indeed the one who gave birth, but she is not a mother, because that which was born did not share in the Spirit of adoption. Likewise, this will be understood regarding sensible mothers and regarding sensible death; for we will call the mother 'the one who gave birth', but the one who gave birth is no longer a mother once the child has died.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The just do not seek to harm the just.
comments.comment: Regarding Prov 17:26, those who are just cannot seek to harm a just man, for they do not seek our things, but us.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A harsh word is a thought or speech that stirs the passions, and a fool who asks about wisdom is wiser than one who wants to know nothing of it.
comments.comment:
Regarding 17:27, he who is sparing of a harsh word is known; but a patient man is wise. He called the thought that moves the passion a harsh word. Or he called the word that moves the passion of his neighbor a harsh word.

Regarding 17:28, when a fool asks for wisdom, wisdom will be calculated; but one making himself appear to be nothing will seem to be wise. If this one asks about wisdom, he is the one desiring to learn something about wisdom; while he who is silent from wisdom is the one desiring to know nothing about wisdom; therefore the former is said to be wiser than the latter.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The man who separates from friends seeks excuses for sins, while the saints are joined to him through virtue, and the fool is led by foolishness.
comments.comment:
Regarding 18:1, a man desiring to separate from friends seeks excuses; but at all times he will be a source of trouble. He says excuses regarding sins; 'for to make excuses is to make excuses in sins,' he says. But he joins all the saints to himself through virtue.

Regarding 18:2, one lacking sense does not need wisdom; for rather he is led by foolishness, for he loved the darkness more than the light.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: He who accepts inherent evil and acts on it marvels at the impious.
comments.comment: Regarding 18:5, to marvel at the face of an impious man is neither good nor holy; the just man turns away in judgment. He who accepts the inherent evil and acts according to it, this one marvels at the face of the impious.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Boldness brings the death that separates us from Christ the life, and meekness, its opposite, brings life.
comments.comment: Regarding 18:6, the lips of a fool lead him into evils; and his mouth calls for his bold death. If death is born from boldness, and death separates the soul from true life, boldness separates us from the one saying, 'I am the life' (John 14:6). And just as death is born from boldness, so life is born from meekness; for meekness is the opposite of boldness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's 'bold death' by contrast with meekness.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: One must first be humbled willingly to reach glory, since whoever lifts himself up will be humbled.
comments.comment: … "Before glory, one is humbled" (Proverbs 18:12). It is necessary first to be humbled voluntarily, so that one may attain glory; for second, glory comes after the un-blinding. For this reason also the Savior said: "The one humbling himself will be lifted up" (Luke 14:11). And behold, "everyone lifting himself up will be humbled" (Matthew 23:12)
comments.selected_reason: Explains the proverb 'before glory one is humbled' in plain terms.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The tongue brings destruction or usefulness depending on how we use it, like a sword that saves or kills according to the one who wields it.
comments.comment: And why, someone says, if this instrument brings us so much destruction, did God put it in us in the beginning? Because it also has great usefulness. And if we are diligent, it has only usefulness and no destruction at all. Listen, then, to what the one who said those earlier things says: "In the hand of the tongue are life and death" (Proverbs 18:21). And Christ shows the same thing when he says: "By your words you will be condemned, and by your words you will be justified" (Matthew 12:37). For the tongue stands in the middle, able to be used for either purpose. You are its master. So too a sword lies in the middle: if you use it against enemies, the instrument has become your salvation; but if you thrust the blow against yourself, it is not the nature of the iron but your own lawlessness that causes the slaughter.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'life and death are in the hand of the tongue' with a clear picture.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: Since words justify or condemn, we must guard the mouth, and the 'hand' of the tongue means its word.
comments.comment: Since 'from the words someone is justified and from his words he is condemned' (Matt 12:37), it is necessary for the mouth to place a guard, so that I may say the good things and not the bad, that we may speak the profitable things and be silent about the harmful ones; for no one is able at once to bring forth words that both justify and condemn. Something like this is said with an enigma in the proverbs: 'Death and life are in the hand of the tongue' (Prov 18:21). And the 'hand' of the 'tongue' is the word.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The boasting of the patient and merciful man is his wisdom, which comes upon the lawless and frees them from wickedness.
comments.comment: A merciful man is patient; but his boasting comes upon the lawless (Proverbs 19:11). If one boasts correctly in the Lord—and our Lord is wisdom—then the one boasting correctly boasts in wisdom. Therefore, the boasting of the patient and merciful one, which is his wisdom and his knowledge, comes upon the lawless, freeing them from wickedness now somewhat imperfectly, but necessarily in the age to come.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The Lord is a consuming fire and angry lion to those who sin, but light and dew to those who walk uprightly.
comments.comment: The threat of a king is like the roar of a lion; but his pleasantness is like dew on grass (Proverbs 19:12). Our Lord becomes a consuming fire and an angry lion toward those sinning, consuming wood, grass, reed, and the flesh that wages war against the spirit; but toward those walking uprightly, He is light and dew, showing them the words of things that have happened and extinguishing the inflamed arrows of the evil one and cooling the heat arising from the practical life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains both images of the verse, the lion's roar and the dew, in terms of how the Lord acts toward sinners and the upright.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Fathers teach their sons virtue and the knowledge of God, but giving wisdom to the children is the Lord's.
comments.comment: It is for the fathers to teach the sons about virtue and the knowledge of the God of the fathers; but to give wisdom to the children is the Lord's (Proverbs 19:14). For there he calls woman wisdom: 'For you have been loved by wisdom, he says, and she will preserve you; honor her, so that she may embrace you' (Proverbs 4:6).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Commandments are called ways as the mind walks in them and testimonies as given before heaven and earth, and one who keeps one preserves his soul.
comments.comment:
The commandments are called commandments as toward the God who commands; but they are called ways as toward the mind walking in them (Proverbs 19:16). And again, because they were given upon the witnesses of heaven and earth, the commandments are called testimonies; therefore also the one receiving them is named a witness, who, having lied about them, will not be without punishment.

He who keeps a commandment preserves his own soul; but he who despises his own ways will perish (Proverbs 19:16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Scripture calls the commandments by different names.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The great loss is the loss of the contemplation of things, and the harm is the ultimate irrationality.
comments.comment:
He who is of a bad mind will suffer much loss; and if he is struck by plague, even his soul...

I think the great loss consists in the deprivation of the contemplation of things, while the addition to the soul is the vanishing of natural conceptions about God, leading it entirely into irrationality. And the Savior says in the Gospels: 'What will a man profit, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul' (Matt 16:26) and 'be harmed' (Matt 16:26). But here the loss shows the ignorance of bodies and incorporeal things; while the harm presents the ultimate irrationality.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The 'later years' mean not time but the purity that follows the practical virtues.
comments.comment: Listen, son, to the instruction of your father, so that you may become wise in your later years (Proverbs 19:20). The 'later years' here does not mean time, but the purity following the practical virtues.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Since the fear of the Lord is life and also instruction and wisdom, and Christ is life, to know instruction and wisdom is to know Christ.
comments.comment: The fear of the Lord is life to a man (Prov 14:27); but the one without fear will slip in places where knowledge is not observed. If 'the fear of the Lord is life to a man' (Prov 14:27) and 'the fear of the Lord is instruction and wisdom' (Prov 1:7), then the life of the man is instruction and wisdom. But Christ says: 'I am the life' (John 14:6); therefore Christ is instruction and wisdom. Thus, 'to know instruction and wisdom' is to know Christ. The one without fear will be in wickedness and ignorance, in which Christ is not.
comments.selected_reason: Reasons from the verse and the Lord's words 'I am the life' to show what the fear of the Lord leads to.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The slothful man will not work his own land, though the practical virtues bring heavenly bread to our mouths.
comments.comment: He who hides his hands in his lap unjustly will not even bring them to his mouth (Proverbs 19:24). He who does not correctly live hides the hands unjustly in his soul, not wishing to work his own land nor to be filled with bread; for the practical virtues have a logic, bringing to our mouths the bread descending from the heavens and giving life to the world.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the slothful man's hidden hands as a refusal to work for spiritual bread.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The foolish become shrewd by seeing a pestilent man scourged, so the punishment of some benefits the salvation of others.
comments.comment: But if you want to take Scripture as witness that sinners are punished also for the training of others, even if these at some time are given up as beyond healing, hear Solomon in the Proverbs saying: 'When a pestilent one is scourged, the foolish becomes more shrewd.' (Proverbs 19:25) He did not say that the one scourged himself will be more shrewd and more prudent through the scourgings, but that the foolish changes from folly to prudence through the scourgings applied to the pestilent one; for this is what the name of shrewdness signifies here. And the foolish changes by seeing others scourged. So it benefits us—if at least we become worthy of salvation through others being punished—the punishment of others.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse: the lesson is learned by the onlooker.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By breaking the law a man dishonors God his Father, and he pushes away his mother, who is instruction.
comments.comment: He who dishonors his father and pushes away his mother will be disgraced and will be a mocker (Proverbs 19:26). Through the transgression of the law he dishonors God, and he pushes away the mother, who is the instruction, if 'a righteous man is born unto life' (Proverbs 11:19). And righteousness consists of all the virtues.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Evil sayings are impure thoughts born in one who has not kept the commandments.
comments.comment: A son left to guard the instruction of a father will meditate on evil sayings (Proverbs 19:27). The impure thoughts are evil sayings being born in the soul of one who has not kept the commandments of the heavenly Father.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Wine and its fury are both unrestrained.
comments.comment: Unrestrained wine and insulting drunkenness (Proverbs 20:1). If 'their wine is the fury of dragons' (Deuteronomy 32:33), then the wine is unrestrained, and therefore the fury is unrestrained, …
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The Nazirites abstain from wine, so they are to be kept from anger.
comments.comment: … anger is insolent; for this is the intoxication that is prone to arise from a boiling spirit. If the Nazirites abstain from wine according to the law, then it has been legislated that the Nazirites be excluded from anger.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: He who is provoked by Christ the King sins against his own soul.
comments.comment: The threat of a king does not differ from the anger of a lion; but he who is provoked by it sins against his own soul. Here Christ has been spoken of in opposition as a king; for he who sins against his own soul by being provoked by this one the king sins.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: As one may borrow grain in a famine, so spiritual grain may be borrowed in the coming age from those who worked.
comments.comment: The one who insults while being lazy is not ashamed; likewise the one who borrows grain in a famine. If it is possible to borrow grain in a famine, it is also possible to borrow spiritual grain in the coming age from those who worked in the six years for their own land and who feed widows and orphans in the seventh year.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Blameless living leaves children blessed through virtue.
comments.comment: He who conducts himself blamelessly in righteousness will leave his children blessed, whom he has made manifest through virtue.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Such a person is rare, and 'pure' means a heart rightly disposed and thinking piously.
comments.comment: But such a person is rare, and because of the difficulty of finding them, they are perhaps thought by some not to exist at all. Furthermore, the rarity is shown by the proverbist saying: 'Who shall boast having a pure heart and shall speak boldly as being free from sin?' (Proverbs 20:9). By saying pure, he means the heart being rightly disposed and thinking concerning piety. He who is persuaded according to the truth, that one has a pure heart. And he who is outside of practical sin speaks boldly as being free from sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'pure heart' means in the verse and why the claim is rare.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A great and small weight is excess and deficiency.
comments.comment: I think that what is called by some a 'great and small weight' is a great excess and deficiency; for both are evils.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'great and small' weights in plain terms as excess and deficiency.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: One who means harm and denies others rest keeps a double measure.
comments.comment: One who intends harm to another, but does not himself intend to allow others to rest, has a double measure, not obeying the commandment which says: 'Whatever you want men to do to you, do likewise to them' (Matt 7:12).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The Lord made the ear and the eye as they hear and see, not as they hear or see badly, which answers those who insult the body and the Creator.
comments.comment: An ear that hears and an eye that sees are both works of the Lord. It is not the eye that sees badly that is the work of the Lord, but the one seeing; nor is it the ear that hears badly the work of the Lord, but the one hearing; and the same must be said concerning the other members of the body. Use this saying against those who slander us, insulting this body and the Creator.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who is to blame when we hear or see badly: the use, not the Creator's work.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Virtues open the eyes of the soul, and wisdom fills us with bread.
comments.comment: Do not love to speak maliciously, so that you may not be caught; but open your eyes and be filled with bread. Through virtues we open the eyes of the soul; and through the wisdom of intelligible things we are filled with bread.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'eyes' and the 'bread' of the verse.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Christ is father to those who have the Spirit by adoption and mother to those who need milk, as Paul was to the Ephesians and Corinthians.
comments.comment: A lamp will be extinguished by one slandering a father or a mother; and the maidens of his eyes will see darkness. The same Christ is able, by intention, to be both father and mother; father to those possessing the Spirit through adoption, and mother to those needing milk and not solid food. For the Christ speaking in Paul became a father to the Ephesians, revealing mysteries of wisdom to them, and a mother to the Corinthians, giving them milk to drink.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A portion studied at first is not blessed at last.
comments.comment: A portion being studied in the first things will not be blessed in the last. 'It parches the throat for a time'; 'later indeed you will find it more bitter, like bile.'
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Do not say in pride that you alone will fight the enemies, but wait on the Lord to help you.
comments.comment: Do not say: 'I will fight the enemy'; but endure the Lord, so that he may help you. Do not say, moved by pride: 'I alone will fight the enemies'; but endure the Lord, so that he may help you. And David says: 'I do not hope in my own bow, nor shall my sword save me' (Psalm 44:6). And again: 'A false horse for salvation' (Psalm 33:17) and 'Unless the Lord builds a house and guards a city' (Ps 127:1).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's command to wait on the Lord, with David's words as support.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A mind made to judge rightly that turns by self-will is the deceitful scale.
comments.comment: A double weight and a deceitful scale are an abomination to the Lord (Prov 11:1). The mind, which is naturally inclined to judge things rightly, but deviates by the inclination of self-will, calls a deceitful scale a 'deceitful scale.'
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A mortal who has not died together with Christ cannot understand the Lord's ways.
comments.comment: The steps of a man are directed by the Lord (Proverbs 20:24); but how can a mortal man understand His ways? A mortal man who has not died together with Christ cannot understand the ways of the Lord.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why a mortal cannot understand his own ways.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Repentance after prayer comes to the unrighteous, so they should promise nothing to God without careful thought.
comments.comment: It is a quick snare for a man to sanctify his own things; for after praying, repentance happens. Repentance toward good things does not happen to the righteous, but to the unrighteous. Let the unrighteous not promise anything to God without careful consideration; for 'after praying, repentance happens.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains the snare of a hasty vow in plain terms.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A wise man separates chaff from wheat, as on a threshing floor.
comments.comment: A wise man is a winnowing fan for an impious king and imposes a threshing floor upon them, separating the chaff from the wheat. 'Make them as a threshing floor' (Proverbs 20:26).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The light of the Lord is the knowledge of the Lord, while the one who seems a lamp in ignorance only empties the mind of good.
comments.comment: The light of the Lord is the breath of men, a lamp that searches the treasury of the belly. If the light of the Lord is the knowledge of the Lord, and the light of the Lord is the breath of men, then the knowledge of the Lord is the breath of men. He named the one who seems to be a lamp in ignorance, emptying the mind of good things and transforming himself into an angel of light (2 Cor 11:14).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Justice and truth please the Lord more than sacrifice of animals.
comments.comment: To do justice and to speak truth is more pleasing to the Lord than the blood of sacrifices: This saying casts out the sacrifice through irrational animals; for a sacrifice to God is a crushed spirit.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why justice and truth are preferred to sacrifice.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Since the mind is among God's works, it was created pure and right.
comments.comment: But His works are pure and right: If the works of God are pure and right, and one of His works is the mind, then the mind was created pure and right by the Lord.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The open-air corner stands against the dusty common house, as virtue against evil, a place of contemplation lit by the sun of righteousness.
comments.comment:
It is better to dwell in a corner of the open air than in dusty places with iniquity (LXX: injustice) and in a common house: He set the open-air corner against the dusty and common house; but if the dusty and common house is evil, the open-air corner is virtue; therefore, an open-air corner is a practice of contemplation, touching and being illuminated by the sun of righteousness.

Paul has spoken well of the high priest of the Jews as a wall having been plastered, to be struck by God; and the Savior in the gospels has spoken of the Pharisees as tombs having been plastered. Also well did he speak of the stone at the corner, where the stone lies which was rejected by the builders and having become a head of the corner; and he has spoken commonly of that which is not of the one God.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Secret gifts are unknown to the left hand.
comments.comment: A secret gift subverts passions: a gift is secret, so that what the right hand does the left hand may not know.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what makes a gift 'secret'.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The gathering of giants is malice and ignorance.
comments.comment: A man wandering from the way of righteousness will rest in a gathering of giants: the gathering of giants is malice and ignorance.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A desert land is virtue free of the old desires, and the contentious woman is malice, which makes the one living with her contentious.
comments.comment: It is better to dwell in a desert land than with a woman angry and contentious: and David says, 'In a desert land and uncultivated and waterless, so I appeared to you in holiness' (Psalm 63:1). A desert land is therefore the virtue which does not have the old men dwelling in it, those decaying according to the desires of deception; … If this is so, is not also the woman who is contentious and talkative and angry malice, which makes the one living with her contentious and talkative and angry.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The wisdom of the Lord rests in the wise man's heart.
comments.comment: A desirable treasure will rest upon the mouth of a wise man: The wisdom of the Lord will rest in the heart of a wise man (Proverbs 15:13, 15:33); but foolish men destroy it.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Wisdom is the fortified city in which the wise dwell, and guarding the mouth and tongue keeps the soul, meaning anger and desire, from trouble.
comments.comment: A wise man ascended fortified cities: Wisdom is a fortified city, in which the wise dwell, pulling down reasonings and every exaltation being lifted up against the knowledge of Christ (2 Corinthians 10:5). He who guards his mouth and his tongue preserves his soul from tribulation: Mouth and tongue, soul and mind; for by 'soul' they mean anger and desire, which some call the passionate part of the soul.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'city' as wisdom and the guarded 'mouth and tongue' as the soul's anger and desire.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The wicked desire evil all the day, meaning through life, while angels never do and men only at times.
comments.comment: An impious man all the day desires evil desires: For angels, never to desire evil desires; for men, sometimes to desire and sometimes not to desire evil desires; but for demons, always to desire evil desires. For 'all the day' signifies through life. Such is also 'be in the fear of the Lord all the day' (Proverbs 23:17), instead of 'through life.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'all the day' as 'through life' and compares angels, men and demons.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Men trust in horses, but the horse is only made ready for battle and salvation is from the Lord.
comments.comment: Again, many think greatly upon a horse, but the God-Word shows that even the conceit of horses is easily broken; for 'these are in chariots and these in horses, but we in the name of the Lord our God shall be magnified' (Ps 20:7). … And also in Proverbs: 'A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but salvation is by the Lord' (Prov 21:31). You see that it is false for salvation, if this does not exist from the Lord, even if it is according to a spoken word.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the horse is no ground for trust.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A name is excellent for the virtue it signifies, so we praise the one who has justice, not one merely called Justice.
comments.comment: A name more excellent than much wealth: He said that the virtue signified by the proper name is beautiful; for this is the beautiful name, which possesses the signified good. In this way, we shall not praise an unjust woman even if she is called justice, but rather the one possessing justice, even if she is named injustice.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what makes a 'name' better than wealth: the good it signifies.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The rich man purifies his anger by almsgiving and the poor man learns humility through poverty.
comments.comment: A rich man and a poor man met one another, and the Lord made both of them equal. The one rich man purifies his anger through almsgiving, cultivating love; the one poor man is trained to be humble through his poverty.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what sense the Lord made rich and poor equal.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Wisdom has four generations: fear, wealth, glory and life.
comments.comment: Four generations of wisdom: fear of the Lord, wealth, glory, and life. 'These are the generations of Noah' (Genesis 6:9), 'these are the generations of Abraham'.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The thorns and thistles the Lord named to Adam are the sins, from which even Christ's crown was struck.
comments.comment: Thorns and snares in crooked paths; but he who guards his own soul will escape them (Proverbs 22:5). And the Lord says to Adam: 'the earth shall bring forth for you thorns and thistles' (Gen 3:18), that is, the soul. Thorns and thistles he calls the sins, from which even the crown of Christ was struck; for he himself bore the sin of the world.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'thorns and snares' as sins.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: In the age to come those enriched in knowledge will rule over those who lack it, though who the servants and masters are is a deeper mystery.
comments.comment:
The rich shall rule the poor, and servants shall lend to their own masters (Proverbs 22:7). In the age to come, those enriched in every way in all knowledge and all wisdom shall rule over the unclean and those deprived of this wealth.

But who are the servants and who are the masters? It is not necessary now to publish this, because the word concerning them is mystical and deeper.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The gifts of a man are his virtues, by which he conquers the devil and his soul is taken from the demons who possessed it.
comments.comment:
God blesses a cheerful and giving man (Prov 22:8a); but the Lord brings to completion the vanity of his works through virtue and knowledge (Prov 22:8b).

The one giving gifts acquires victory and honor (Prov 22:9a), but his soul is taken away from what he has possessed. The gifts of a man are called virtues, through which, conquering the devil, he offers himself as an honor to God, and his soul is taken away from the demons who had possessed it.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Solomon wishes to cast out the pestilence, meaning the devil, from the soul by spiritual teaching, since the soul is a council.
comments.comment: 'Cast out a pestilence from the council, and strife shall come out with him' (Prov 22:10); for when he sits in a council, he dishonors all. He spoke of the most critical state, from which the wise Solomon wishes to cast out the man through spiritual teaching; and the strife signifies contention. He may also mean a pestilence and the devil, whom it is necessary to drive away from the soul. For if he sits in it, through impurity he dishonors all the righteous thoughts. And the apostle also shows the soul as a council, into which he introduces accusing thoughts and defending ones; … where there is accusation and defense, there is also a council.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'pestilence' is and why he must be cast out of the soul.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Christ the King shepherds us through spiritual knowledge, which the one who breaks his law despises.
comments.comment:
A king shall rule with his lips (Prov 22:11); and the eyes of the Lord shall preserve perception (Prov 22:12); but the lawless one makes words contemptible.

The Lord himself is the shepherd of our souls and through spiritual knowledge he shepherds us, a knowledge which he who transgresses his law despises. It should be noted that since Christ is king, he is said to shepherd us through his condescension; 'for I,' he says, 'am the good shepherd' (John 10:11). But if he is a king among kings and a shepherd of sheep, he will at some time be only a king, as a dignity for those sheep who have transitioned into the kingdom.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The sluggard fears the devil, the lion in the roads, and rises to meet him in virtue.
comments.comment: The enemy, the devil, is seen to say: 'a lion in the roads, and murderers in the streets' (Proverbs 26:13); our enemy the devil prowls about like a lion seeking someone to devour, whom the sluggard, fearing him, rises up to meet in the work of virtues.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'lion in the roads' is.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: One hated by the Lord falls into the pit; Job fell through testing, not hatred.
comments.comment: 'A deep pit, the mouth of the lawless' (Proverbs 22:14); but he who is hated by the Lord will fall into it. Job, not being hated by the Lord, but on account of testing, fell into it (Job 5:7).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The rod from the root of Jesse is far from the heart of the foolish.
comments.comment: 'Folly spreads from the heart of a youth; but a rod and instruction are far from him' (Prov 22:15); far from the heart of the foolish is the rod which is from the root of Jesse (Isa 11:1).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: As the devil slanders us, so we slander him and Christ, giving our virtues to the rich Satan to our own loss.
comments.comment: 'The slanderer's poverty does many of his own evils; but he gives to the rich upon less' (Proverbs 22:16); just as the devil slanders us, taking from us the virtues which he did not give to us, so also we slander him, taking from him the evils which we did not give to him. And just as we take from him the evils, as if from a poor man we take in virtues; so also we give our virtues to him at a loss, as if to a rich man we give in evil. One of the elders was saying that we are the slanderers, slandering Christ, having made him poor through us, even though he owes nothing to us, and taking much from him and giving to Satan upon the humiliation of our souls.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: He who hears God's words is the one who does what they command.
comments.comment: 'Compare your ear with the words of the wise and hear my word; and examine your own heart, so that you may know that they are good' (Proverbs 22:17); this one hears the words of God, the one doing the things commanded by them; 'for not the hearers of the law are righteous before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified' (Romans 2:13).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to give one's ear to the words of the wise.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: He who broadens his heart through purity will understand God's words, practical, natural and theological.
comments.comment: 'And you also shall write them down for yourself thrice for counsel and knowledge upon the breadth of your heart'; he who broadens his heart through purity will perceive the words of God, both the practical, the natural, and the theological. …
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The layer under the sides of the soul is virtue, which is taken from those who cannot restore their bad thoughts through good ones.
comments.comment: … Regarding Proverbs 24:8, 26: 'Do not give yourself as a surety, being ashamed of your face'; and 24:27: 'For if you do not have something from which to spread it, the layer under your sides shall be taken.' Those who entertain bad thoughts and thus honor the evil one should strive to whatever power they can through good thoughts to restore the bad ones. For if they are not able to do this, the layer under the sides of the soul—that is, virtue—shall be taken. For this is called the garment of the mind when it stands in righteousness, but it is called a cushion when the rest has fallen due to bad thoughts.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: To move the bounds of a virtue is to fall into a fault on either side, as with godliness and courage.
comments.comment: Regarding Proverbs 24:28: 'Do not move the eternal boundaries which your fathers set.' He who moves the boundaries of godliness demonstrates either superstition or impiety, and he who moves the boundaries of courage achieves either rashness or cowardice. Likewise, this should be considered regarding the other virtues, regarding the dogmas, and regarding faith itself. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the ancient landmark as the bounds of each virtue, with plain examples.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The table of a powerful man stands for Scripture, which must be understood spiritually, since knowledge of the story alone is not true.
comments.comment: Regarding Proverbs 23:1: 'If you sit to dine at the table of a powerful man, observe mindfully what is set before you...' and 23:3: 'But if you are more gluttonous, do not desire his delicacies'; for these things possess a false life. For not everyone contains the more mystical intellect of the Scripture. It is necessary that the Divine Scripture be understood mindfully and spiritually; for sensory knowledge according to the history is not true.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Goodness falls away only through the person's own carelessness, and one fed by the living bread has his wing restored.
comments.comment: Such goodness would never fall away from one who takes in, so to speak, the living bread (John 6:51) to preserve himself. If it falls away from anyone, it falls away through his own fault, because he grew careless about partaking of the living bread and the true drink (John 6:55). Fed and watered by these, the wing is restored, as the most wise Solomon also says, speaking of the man who is truly rich: “For he has made himself wings like an eagle’s, and he returns to the house of the one who is set over him” (Proverbs 23:5).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Do not dine with a coarse man, because his impiety and lawlessness defile spiritual knowledge.
comments.comment: Regarding Proverbs 23:6: 'Do not dine with a coarse man'; nor desire his foods; 23:7: 'For in whatever way anyone swallows hair, so he eats and drinks'; 23:8: 'Nor let him be brought to you, and eat your bread with him'; for he will vomit him out and will defile your beautiful words.
