If the coarse man eats the grain of impiety and drinks lawless wine, one must not dine with him; therefore, it is not right to be impious and lawless, for these vices defile spiritual knowledge.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the warning against sharing a table in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: What is deep and mystical should not be told to a fool.
comments.comment: Regarding Proverbs 23:9: 'Say nothing into the ears of a fool' … 'Say nothing wise,' that is to say, profound and mystical; for it is not fitting to cast pearls before swine.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the proverb forbids speaking to a fool.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Wickedness is what deprives orphans of their Father in heaven.
comments.comment: Regarding the boundaries: 'Do not shift the eternal boundaries which your fathers set,' and 'Do not enter the estate of orphans,' for wickedness is that by which they were deprived of their Father in heaven.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Fear of the Lord turns us from evil, so we are told to keep it all our days.
comments.comment: Regarding jealousy: 'Let not your heart envy sinners,' but be in the fear of the Lord all your days. Since it is said, 'All turns away from evil by the fear of the Lord' (Proverbs 16:6), it rightly exhorts us to turn away from all evil throughout our whole life.
comments.selected_reason: A clear explanation of why the proverb tells us to keep the fear of the Lord.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The offspring of a soul are right reasonings and spiritual contemplations; a soul without them is barren.
comments.comment: Regarding offspring: 'If you keep these, you shall have offspring,' and 'your hope shall not be disappointed.' The mind has said that the right reasonings and the spiritual contemplations are offspring. Therefore, the soul is barren which does not have these offspring, which it is nature to bring forth from the spiritual bridegroom.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A torn and ragged garment cannot be a wedding garment.
comments.comment: Regarding drunkenness and fornication: 'Every drunkard and fornicator shall be poor, and shall clothe himself in torn and ragged things.' There is no wedding garment that is torn and ragged.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The mother of the mind is the passionate part of the soul, which leads the mind into light through the practical virtues.
comments.comment: Regarding the mother: 'Listen, son, to the father of him who begot you, and do not despise that your mother has grown old.' One of the elders heard someone saying the soul is the mother of the mind; for this, he says, leads the mind into light through the practical virtues. The 'soul' referred to was the passionate part of the soul, which is divided into spirit and desire.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: These wines come from the vine of Sodom.
comments.comment: Regarding wines: 'Not of those who intoxicate with wines? Not of those who track where the drinking takes place?' These wines are from the vine of Sodom.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Conversing while walking, the mind walks worthily of its calling.
comments.comment: Regarding fellowship: 'Do not get drunk with wine, but converse with righteous men, and converse in your walkings.' The Mind, conversing in walkings, walks worthily of the calling wherewith he was called.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: What the eyes take in from outside, the mouth then speaks.
comments.comment: Regarding eyes and cups: 'If you give your eyes to bowls and cups.' Sin resembles a bowl according to thought, and a cup according to energy. Regarding nakedness: 'Later you will walk more naked than the proud.' The proud knock much and do not open the place they knock at. But to the disciples the Lord says, 'Knock and it shall be opened to you' (Matthew 7:7). Regarding the eyes and mouth: 'Your eyes, when they see something foreign, your mouth then will speak.'
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A mind that takes in a foreign thought is like a pilot tossed by every wind until the dawn of recognizing sin.
comments.comment:
… A mind having received an alien thought will meditate on evil logismoi (thoughts). But he who guards himself will inherit life.

And it will lie still, just as in the heart of a sea, and just as a pilot in a great swell, being tossed by every wind of instruction (Proverbs 23:34).

When will the dawn be, so that coming, I may seek with those with whom I will be gathered? The dawn of the soul is the recognition of sin (Proverbs 23:35).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Those who lose the faith do not fight the opposing spirits after steering, and the same shipwreck can befall every virtue, so life on earth is a naval battle.
comments.comment:
After steering comes war, but help comes with a deliberative heart. Those shipwrecking regarding faith do not fight against the opposing spirits in war with steering (Proverbs 24:6).

It is also possible to say this regarding every virtue; for there is also shipwreck regarding temperance, and regarding love, and regarding freedom from greed; and regarding each doctrine, similarly, it becomes a shipwreck according to the catholic and apostolic church. If, however, one must fight against the adversaries after steering, life upon the earth is near to us as a naval battle.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Practical virtues are the gates through which God's wisdom enters.
comments.comment: Wisdom and good understanding in the gates of the wise (Proverbs 24:7). The gates of the wise are the practical virtues through which the wisdom of God enters.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear, short meaning of the gates of the wise.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Impurity stains a man until vice is corrected either by practical discipline or by the punishment of severity.
comments.comment: Impurity will stain a man like a plague (Prov 26:10), in a day of evil and in a day of tribulation, until it fails away. If vice diminishes virtue, and showing that virtue corrupts vice; this indeed will happen in the age to come, until vice fails away. For it has been set to stain instead of corrupting; but impurity is corrupted, either by practical discipline or by the punishment of severity (Prov 26:11).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The word is for those given knowledge who neglect instruction and are led by vice to death.
comments.comment: To rescue those being led unto death and those being driven out to be slain, let him not spare. This is the word for those being made worthy of knowledge and those neglecting instruction, many of whom are led by vice unto death (Proverbs 24:11).
comments.selected_reason: Gives a short, plain application of the call to rescue those led to death.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Anyone who wishes may eat the honey of the divine writings, but the wax is for the pure alone.
comments.comment: Eat honey, O son, for it is a good thing, so that your throat may be sweetened (Proverbs 24:13). He who benefits from the divine writings eats honey; but he who casts out the words from those very things from which even the holy prophets and apostles have received, chews wax. And to eat honey is possible for everyone who wishes, but the wax is for the pure alone (Proverbs 24:13).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the honey of the verse as the benefit of Scripture.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: God turns his anger from the fallen, but is angry with one who is proud over his enemy's fall, for this is to be like the devil.
comments.comment:
Do not rejoice over your enemy, nor exult in his stumbling, for the Lord will see and it will not please him, and he will turn his anger away from him. God indeed turns his anger away from the fallen one having had mercy on him, but he is angry with the one who has become proud over the fall of his enemy.

For everyone who rejoices over a perishing soul is like the devil, who does not want all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. It should be noted, however, that he spoke of a human being here, for whom the Lord has enjoined us to pray in the Gospels (Matthew 5:44).
comments.selected_reason: Clearly explains why we must not rejoice over an enemy's fall.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Evil does not produce virtues and right doctrines, but those who fear the Lord have offspring all day long.
comments.comment: Evil offspring will not be produced, but the light of the ungodly will be extinguished. Bad virtues and doctrines will not be produced—for these are the offspring of the soul—because they do not fear the Lord; but those who are in the fear of the Lord will have offspring all day long, and their hope will not fail.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The ungodly will be extinguished suddenly; punishment is the deprivation of the knowledge of God, while judgment is the distribution of an age.
comments.comment: Fear God, son, and the King, and do not disobey either of them, 'so that they may know you, the only true God, and whom you sent, Jesus Christ' (John 4:24). For the ungodly will be extinguished suddenly; and who will know the punishments of both? How then does the Savior say in the Gospels: 'The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son' (John 5:22)? Either punishment is one thing, and judgment is another. Punishment is indeed the deprivation of impassibility and the knowledge of God with bodily distress; but judgment is the distribution of an age according to each of the rational bodies.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The good blessing is the intellectual one, not the sensory.
comments.comment: But those who rebuke others will appear better; and a good blessing will come upon them. The good blessing is the intellectual one, which is distinguished from the sensory blessing.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The field to prepare is the mind alone, and a house is built with wisdom, which does not enter a poorly crafted soul.
comments.comment:
Prepare your works for the exodus and prepare for the field. Our Lord in the Gospels named the world a field; but Solomon now has spoken of the field as the theory of the world. But the field in the Gospels is that of the existing composition of a human soul and body, for it is sensory; whereas the field indicated here is of the mind alone, being intellectual and understood from these words of the world, into which pure hearts enter.

And go after me and you will rebuild your house, 'for a house is built with wisdom' (Prov 24:3); 'but into a poorly-crafted soul wisdom will not enter.' If you leave him, he will become a wasteland and will wither and become abandoned; and the barriers of his stones will be dug up. A barrier is apatheia of the rational soul, established from the practical virtues.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Those who possess the glory of God hide his word within themselves, so as not to sin and to honor the commands.
comments.comment: The glory of God hides a word (Proverbs 25:2): he who possesses the glory of God, he called the glory of God, and he who possesses the glory of the heavenly King, he named the glory of a king; for these hide the word of God within themselves, so that they might not sin, and they honor the commands through which they perform them. … Or perhaps he says 'the glory of God' regarding the one glorifying God, and 'the glory of a king' regarding the one glorifying the king…
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The rod stands for punishment.
comments.comment: 'A whip for the horse, a goad for the ox, and a rod for the fool' (Proverbs 26:3). The rod is now a symbol of punishment.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Holy words and knowledge are wasted on a fool, as a stone is worthless in a golden sling.
comments.comment: He who sends a word through a foolish messenger makes a dream out of his own feet: 'Do not give holy things to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine' (Matthew 7:6). Removing the path of the legs and the proverb from the mouth of fools: 'Remove the evil path of the fool, and make a long distance of false knowledge from him.' He who releases a stone from a sling is like one giving glory to a fool: 'Knowledge does not suit a fool, and a stone is worthless in a golden sling' (Proverbs 26:8).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The hand in which thorns grow means the actions by which one sins, not the body part.
comments.comment: And we have the 'hands' signifying actions in the scripture, as this one also seems to have understood. For when it says: 'thorns grow in the hand of the drinker' (Proverbs 26:9), we do not take the part of the body to mean—for thorns do not grow upon that—but rather the actions, according to which one sins.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the hand of the drinker means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: If the ecstasy of fools is crushed, they become pure and approach God, for all flesh shall see his salvation.
comments.comment: Much is covered by the flesh of fools, for their ecstasy is crushed. If the ecstasy of fools, by which they were beside themselves for God (cf. 2 Corinthians 5:13), is crushed, having become pure again, they approach God; for 'all flesh shall see the salvation of God.' One must note here that he named the thickened souls from the evil flesh of fools. So also the Lord says: 'My spirit shall not remain in these men because they are flesh' (cf. Genesis 6:3).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A fool who returns to the wickedness he cast off is like a dog eating its vomit.
comments.comment: Like a dog when it rushes upon its own vomit and becomes loathsome, so a fool, having turned back to his own sin by his own wickedness, is like a dog eating its own vomit after casting away his wickedness and turning again toward it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the proverb of the dog and its vomit in plain terms.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: One who hides righteousness with unrighteousness will not eat from the tree of life.
comments.comment: Having hidden a sluggish hand in his lap, he will not be able to bring it to the mouth. If 'a tree of life grows from the fruits of righteousness' (cf. Proverbs 11:30), everyone hiding righteousness with unrighteousness will not eat from this tree.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear reading of the sluggard's hidden hand.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Presiding over another's judgment is like holding a dog's leash.
comments.comment: Like one holding a dog's leash, so is the one presiding over another's judgment. Use this saying for those being voted for some unworthy ones in Jerusalem or by lot (cf. Proverbs 26:17).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Satan flatters us or shouts like one defeated, and he is not to be obeyed, for seven evils lie in his heart.
comments.comment:
Smooth lips cover a sad heart. A pure heart will not seize sadness; for he has driven away corrupt desires from it.

If the enemy entreats you with a loud voice, do not be persuaded by him. Our Satan sometimes entreats us, tickling us through unclean thoughts and throwing himself upon us with the smoothness of pleasure, and sometimes indeed raising a voice truly loud as if having been defeated, one whom one must not obey having the war against us.

For there are seven evils in his heart. These evils oppose the seven spirits.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the enemy's smooth and loud speech and why not to trust it.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A man estranged from the virtue and knowledge of his heart falls into wickedness and ignorance and becomes a slave.
comments.comment:
Like a bird when it falls from its own nest, so a man is enslaved when he is made a stranger from his own places.

Virtue and knowledge are of the heart, from which being estranged a man falls into wickedness and ignorance and becomes a slave, since 'everyone practicing sin is a slave of sin' (John 8:34). The heart is delighted by perfumes, wines, and incenses; but the soul is shattered by accidents. The impassive Mind delights in diverse wisdom; but the empassioned mind will fall into ignorance.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the bird fallen from its nest as a soul cut off from its own place of virtue.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The better friend is the one joined to me through true knowledge rather than only through nature.
comments.comment: Do not abandon your friend and your fellow-countryman; 'They have left me the spring of living water and have dug for themselves cisterns' (Jeremiah 2:13). Do not enter the house of your brother in misfortune; such was the one who entered the wedding feasts and did not have wedding clothes (Matthew 22:11). A near friend is better than a brother far from home. Better is the one joined to me through true knowledge than the one joined to me only through nature.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the near friend of the verse is.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: What the insolent plunders is, in the Gospel's words, taken from the one who has not: the remnants of virtue and knowledge misused.
comments.comment: Take away his garment, for an insolent man passes by who plunders what belongs to others. This is that which is said in the Gospel: 'And from him who has not, even what he seems to have will be taken away' (Luke 8:18). This shows, in my opinion, the intellectual remnants of virtues and the knowledge of God being taken from men who have used them badly.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Our Lord is the fig tree.
comments.comment: 'He who plants a fig tree shall eat its fruits' (Proverbs 27:18): Our Lord is the fig tree, for its fruit heals leprosy.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Many who plant a sensible fig tree never eat its fruit, but he who eats the fruits of a spiritual tree eats alone and for all.
comments.comment: Regarding the fig thus given, the proverb says: 'He who plants a fig tree will eat its fruits, but he who guards the Lord will be honored' (Proverbs 27:18), which is not contrary to history; for many having planted a sensible fig tree neither sat down nor ate its fruits, either being prevented by death or being driven far away from the plant they planted, while only he who eats the fruits of a spiritual tree eats alone and for all.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the fig tree as a spiritual tree whose fruit is not lost to death or exile.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Hearts differ as faces do, both among those inclined to good and among those who rush toward evil.
comments.comment: Since “just as faces are not like faces, so neither are hearts like the hearts of men” (Proverbs 27:19), it is clear that there would be differences in “the hearts of men” both among those who have inclined toward the good, since they have not all been stamped and shaped toward it equally and alike, and among those who through neglect of the good rush toward the opposite. For among these also wickedness is poured out in great measure in some, and in others to a lesser degree.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that hearts, like faces, differ in goodness and in wickedness.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Not dishonoring the fool will not remove his foolishness but teaches him what dishonor foolishness brings.
comments.comment: 'If one dishonors a fool in the midst of a sitting, you will not take away his foolishness from him' (Proverbs 27:22): Not dishonoring the fool will not remove him from foolishness, but rather teaching him what kind of dishonor foolishness becomes to a stranger.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Attend to yourself and direct your virtues, because men do not always stay strong in them, and shepherds of the churches must attend to hearts.
comments.comment:
'Knowingly shepherd your souls' (Proverbs 27:23): Attend to yourself and direct your virtues, for men do not always remain equally strong in them; nor do they transition healthily from virtue to virtue or from knowledge to knowledge, those not easily receiving the human condition...; for he says 'generations' regarding virtues and knowledges, according to which the saints are born, and he shows this through what he writes: 'A generation of wisdom: the fear of the Lord, and riches, and glory, and life' (Proverbs 22:4).

This proverb should also be used toward the shepherds of the churches, to whom it is necessary to attend not to faces but to hearts, and to shepherd the sheep intellectually.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the call to know the state of one's flock as care for virtues and hearts.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The field is the mind, the green things are the virtues within it, and tending them yields the knowledge of God.
comments.comment: 'Tend the green things in the field and shear the wool' (Song of Sol 2:16/4:16): He calls the mind a field, and the green things are the virtues existing within it by potentiality; the one tending them shears the wool, which is a symbol of the knowledge of God, which he also again calls a mountain pasture; for a mountain pasture is the knowledge of the holy powers, fitting the more irrational state of souls. It is the custom of Scripture to call the saints 'mountains.' Thus also David lifts his soul up to the mountains, whence his help shall come (Ps 121:1); and again, 'the mountains like rams, and the bulls like lambs of the flock, for the salvation of Israel' (Psalm 114:4); for if angels rejoice over one repentant person, how much more over a multitude traveling from evil toward virtue.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The arrogant ruler lives in fear of death, but the diligent one who knows it is better to be with Christ is hopeful.
comments.comment: Therefore, even if the ruler acts arrogantly, his life and his years turn out to be few, and he always has fear in his ears because of the uncertainty of the manner of death. Such a person has a fearful nature. For when he is in care regarding life, he reveres even death. But the diligent one, knowing that it is better 'to depart and be with Christ' (Phil 1:23), is hopeful, not being such as the wicked, but one who fears; for it has been said that 'the impious flees when no one pursues' (Prov 28:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One brave in impiety slanders the poor, while one brave in virtue exhorts them.
comments.comment: A man who slanders the poor in impieties: If he is brave in impieties, he is brave also in virtues; and if the brave man slanders the poor in impieties, the brave man in virtues exhorts the poor; surely everyone who exhorts the poor is brave in pieties.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Those who love and practice the law gain dispassion and the knowledge of God, which is the wall that guards the rational nature.
comments.comment: But those who love the law surround themselves with a wall: Everyone who loves the law practices the law, and everyone who practices the law acquires dispassion and the knowledge of God; if then those who love the law surround themselves with a wall, now the wall signifies dispassion and the knowledge of God, which alone is suited to guard the rational nature.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wall around those who love the law.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The mind that shepherds passions by transgressing the law dishonors God.
comments.comment: He who shepherds profligacy dishonors his father: He calls the mind a shepherd, and the passions within it are sheep, which he nourishes within himself through the transgression of the law, thereby dishonoring God; for profligacy is a sickness of the soul, consisting of passionate thoughts carried out through the body; but profligacy of the mind is the assumption of false dogmas and contemplations.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The righteous and wise destroy the wickedness that is the wealth of the impious by leading the impure toward virtue.
comments.comment: He who increases his wealth through usury and abundance brings it to the one who shows mercy to the poor: If the wealth of the impious is wickedness, and wise men will destroy it, it is evident that the righteous and wise are destroying wickedness by leading the impure toward virtue through spiritual teaching. …
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: He who covers his impiety will not prosper, but he who confesses it is forgiven and loved.
comments.comment: 'He who covers his impiety will not prosper; but he who explains and reproves will be loved' (Proverbs 28:13). And David: 'I said, he says, I will confess to the Lord my iniquity, and you forgave the impiety of my heart' (Psalm 32:5); and 'speak first of your iniquities.'
comments.selected_reason: Joins the proverb to David's confession and forgiveness.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: He who guarantees Satan guarantees injustice, promising to pay him its fruits.
comments.comment: A man who guarantees a murderer will be a fugitive and will not be in safety. He who guarantees Satan guarantees injustice, promising to pay him the fruits of injustice. Concerning this, the Gospel also says that one defiled through murder and strife is put into prison.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: He who purifies himself will be filled with knowledge, but the unclean with ignorance.
comments.comment: He who works his own land will be filled with bread; but he who pursues leisure will be filled with want (Proverbs 28:19). He who purifies himself will be filled with knowledge; but the unclean will be filled with ignorance.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear spiritual reading of working one's own land.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The faces of the righteous are the virtues, and one who is not ashamed of the virtues is not good.
comments.comment: He who is not ashamed before the faces of the righteous is not good; such a man will be given a crust of bread instead of a man (Proverbs 28:21). If the virtues are the faces of the righteous, he is not good who is not ashamed of the virtues. And if the vices are the faces of the sinners, he is good who is not ashamed of the vices.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Those who are now merciful will be shown mercy and, as angels, will rule over the ungodly, even making the ruler merciful.
comments.comment: A wealthy man hastens to be rich, and does not know that mercy will rule him (Proverbs 28:22). Those who are now merciful will, in the age to come, be shown mercy by God and, having become angels, will rule over the ungodly. Such a status was also promised to his disciples, that the Lord would give them to sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matthew 19:28). And a throne is that in which the mind sits, a spiritual knowledge gathering together those who have wandered from godliness. And to judge here means to teach, as also 'open your mouth with the word of God and judge all healthily,' instead of teaching. It is also to be understood that the merciful one, having conquered the ruler, himself will not become a ruler, but will rather make the ruler merciful.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the mercy that will rule the one who hastens to be rich.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The destruction of the ungodly means the removal of impiety, so they become righteous.
comments.comment: The righteous stand in the places of the ungodly; and in their destruction the righteous will be multiplied (Proverbs 28:28). … They being impious, they shall become righteous; for the destruction now signifies the removal of impiety. Thus also Matthew, having lost the tax collector, the Lord granted righteousness to him (Matt 9:13).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the destruction of the ungodly means.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: There is no healing while the stubborn man is still burning, though health may come after the ember.
comments.comment: A man rebuking a stubborn man is better (Prov 29:1); for when he is burning, there will be no healing. He did not say that when the flame has ceased there is no healing, but that while he is burning there will be no healing, as one having wood, grass, or reed still present, even if health happens to come to those being burned after the ember.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: All who are under the rulers of this darkness groan under impious rulers.
comments.comment: When a righteous man is praised, peoples will rejoice; but when impious rulers rule, men groan (Prov 29:2). All those who are under the authorities and the powers and the cosmic rulers of this darkness, these certainly also groan.
comments.selected_reason: Names who groans under impious rulers.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: He who nurtures wickedness loses knowledge; or the shepherd's passionate thoughts are goats and his dispassionate ones sheep.
comments.comment: A man loving wisdom, his father rejoices; but he who pastures prostitutes will lose wealth (Prov 29:3). And he who nurtures wickedness will lose knowledge. Alternatively: A good mind is a shepherd having possessed passionless thoughts, and an evil mind is a shepherd having possessed passionate thoughts. And if this is so, is not a passionate thought a goat, and is not a passionless thought a sheep? Therefore also the Lord sets the goats on the left and the sheep on the right; and he says 'goats and sheep' regarding those possessing goats and sheep, that is, those having passionate and passionless thoughts. In the same way, regarding those having the weeds, he commanded 'weeds', and regarding those having the grain, 'grain', naming them from the most inferior and most excellent state. Such is also what is said by Paul, 'love does not wander' (1 Corinthians 13:8), instead of 'he who has love'.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Christ lifts up the rational nature; the antichrist overthrows it.
comments.comment: A righteous king lifts up a land; but an unlawful man overthrows it (Prov 29:4). Christ lifts up the rational nature; but the antichrist overthrows it.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a short, clear reading of the righteous king and the unlawful man.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Lack of discernment is real poverty.
comments.comment: A discerning mind does not exist even for a poor man. Truly, one without discernment is poor.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The enraged fool is laughed at, like the man who did not make God his helper.
comments.comment: A wise man judges nations; but a foolish man, being enraged, is laughed at and does not fall. 'And at him, says David, they shall laugh and say: Behold a man who did not set God as his helper' (Psalm 52:7).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: He seeks the soul of the righteous who wants to understand things as thought.
comments.comment: Men sharing in blood will seek the holy; but the upright will seek his soul. He who seeks the soul of the righteous is the one desiring to understand things as they have been thought.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The wise man stores up his passion in measure, either by being angry at wrongs done to the righteous or by long-suffering.
comments.comment: A fool pours out his whole passion; but a wise man stores up his passion in measure. This one stores up his passion in measure, that is, he who is enraged at things concerning the righteous, or he who consumes his passion in measure through long-suffering. And to the simpler ones, one should speak the former, but to the serious ones, the latter.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to store up one's passion in measure.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: To the lawless there will be no interpreter but a punisher, with a rod instead of a word.
comments.comment: An interpreter shall not exist for a nation that is lawless; but he who keeps the law is blessed. To those who have kept the law, an interpreter shall exist; but to those who have acted lawlessly, an interpreter shall not exist, but a punisher shall exist; if not by word, then by rod; a rod is given to a lawless nation.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the absence of an interpreter as the lawless receiving the rod instead of the word.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: No one is harsh by nature, and Pharaoh shows that the hardened are instructed by scourging, not by words.
comments.comment: A harsh servant will not be instructed by words; for even if he understands, he will not obey. Because no one is harsh by nature, he demonstrates 'for even if he understands, he will not obey'; for the one who is harsh by nature could never understand anything right. I say this because of Pharaoh, having been hardened against Israel, being instructed not by words, but by scourging.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the harsh servant by the example of Pharaoh.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Everyone who squanders is a slave of sin, since everyone who sins is a slave of sin.
comments.comment: He who squanders from childhood will be a servant; but at the last he will grieve for himself. If squandering makes one sin, 'for everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin' (John 8:34), then everyone who squanders is a slave of sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the squanderer becomes a servant.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The oath of the law sets God in the soul, and one who hears it and does not confess his sins is turned aside by fear of men.
comments.comment:
He who divides the truth is hated by his own soul. 'The thief,' he says, 'does not come except in order to steal and slaughter and destroy' (John 10:10).

If, however, having an oath set forth, they hear it and do not disclose the sin, they will be turned aside by fear and shame of men. The Oath spoke the law; for just as the oath places God in the soul, so also the law introduces God into the soul; and in whatever way perjury again annuls God from the soul, so also lawlessness casts God out from it. If, therefore, he says, having heard the law set forth, they do not confess their sins, 'they will be turned aside by fear and shame of men.' Thus also David says: 'I swore and I stood to keep your judgments of righteousness' (Psalm 119:106).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: In doing right we treat the angels who lead us, and justice will come to us from the Lord on the day of judgment.
comments.comment: Many treat the faces of leaders; but from the Lord, justice happens to the man. In acting rightly, we treat the angels; for they are our leaders having taken us from the beginning, 'when the Most High divided the nations' (Deut 32:8) and 'he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of his angels' (Deut 32:8). And the justice from the judgment will be for us from the Lord on that day when he judges the inhabited world in righteousness (Acts 17:31), if indeed the Father has given all judgment to the Son.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: He is the most foolish of men because he lacks human wisdom.
comments.comment: For I am the most foolish of all men, and there is no human wisdom in me. The Foolish One said this by way of the lack of human wisdom.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: No one has ascended into heaven except the Son of Man, who gathered the nations into the knowledge of God and the virtues.
comments.comment:
Who ascended into heaven and descended? 'No one has ascended into heaven above, except the Son of Man who descended from heaven' (John 3:13).

Who gathered the winds in a bosom? Who wetted water in a garment? Who grasped all the ends of the earth? By what faith or in what way did he gather those 'from the east and the west and the north and the sea' (Psalm 107:3) into the knowledge of God and have given to them a spiritual vision to deposit in the virtues? And in another way: Who through true knowledge hid false knowledge? Who deposited true knowledge in the virtues? Who 'from the east and the west and the north and the sea' (Psalm 107:3) gathered all the nations, making them dense with the virtues and depositing the heavenly water, the flowing from the spring of life?
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: God's words may not be added to or taken from, lest you be found false.
comments.comment: Do not add to his words, so that he may not examine you and you become false; for by the law of the Lord, 'it is not permitted to add, and it is not permitted to take away' (Deuteronomy 4:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the command not to add to God's words by the law of Deuteronomy.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: He asks to be kept from false knowledge, and says that those who believe in Christ are heirs, not thieves, of the insights of the prophets and apostles.
comments.comment:
Make a vain word and a long false word far from me. Make a pseudonymous knowledge far from me.

So that, not being filled, I may not become false and say: 'Who sees me?' Or, being in need, I may steal and swear by the name of God. Lest, he says, being filled, a proud listener of knowledge I become and say: 'No one shall know my wisdom.' Lest, being filled with unapproachable knowledge, I appear to men as a liar, saying such things which those endowed with blood and flesh are not able to know.

And the following is also well-added: 'so that, not being in need, I may not steal and swear by the name of God'; for someone steals foreign theories so that he may fill his mind while starving. But this happened before the coming of the Savior; now Paul says: 'let him who steals steal no longer' (Eph 4:28), but rather let him work righteousness.

so that having acquired knowledge, one may share it with the one in need. For what indeed is that which is not ours, so that we, who have believed in Christ, should steal? For all things are ours, but we belong to Christ, through whom all things came to be, and Christ belongs to God (1 Corinthians 3:23).

He who steals knowledge is not the one taking from the one who previously possessed it, but the one who subtracts knowledge from a false name. For all those who have believed in Christ, receiving insights from the holy prophets and apostles, are not called thieves of others' insights, but rather heirs of ancestral goods.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The mind must not hand itself to evil again, being a slave of sin.
comments.comment: Do not hand over a servant into the hands of a master, lest he curse you and you be destroyed. Flee, mind, lest you hand over yourself to evil again, if 'everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin' (John 8:34).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The crows that mystically nourish the righteous gouge out the eyes of the unrighteous who mocked the Father and dishonored ancient knowledge.
comments.comment: Mocking the eye of a father and dishonoring the aged mother, crows cut him out of the ravines (Proverbs 30:17): these crows mystically nourish the righteous, but they slaughter the unrighteous, gouging out the eyes of injustice, because they mocked the Father and God of all, and dishonored the ancient knowledge that begot them; and regarding the crows that gouge out the eyes of the impious, he called them ravens, but regarding those devouring him entirely, he named them eagles, because they believe in a partial purification for the former, and a total purification for the latter.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The ravens that dig out the eye are not to be taken by history, for slander of parents is everywhere but ravens are not.
comments.comment: … concerning a father or mother being spoken ill of, it has been said: 'Ravens tore him from the cliffs and young eagles devoured him' (Proverbs 30:17), which would not be according to history, since slandering parents is found everywhere, while ravens are not found everywhere; but it is clear that, being held by this error under dark energies, he is in some way subdued and devoured, those which, being lowly, are accustomed to wear away a crevice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Life's affairs are vanity, like a ship always at sea, so the paths of men cannot be grasped.
comments.comment: [The ship] goes through the sea, and does so always, thrown off balance by opposing winds. And since life’s affairs are vanity—people always at sea, and no one advancing into eternal life—their paths cannot be grasped. So of the famous kings of the earth, or rulers too, no work foreign to piety is left after death; their glory has gone out.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The ways of a man in youth are not recognized, inflamed by desire; so too the adulterous soul that left her bridegroom.
comments.comment: He also says the ways of a man during youth are not recognized, inflamed by desires because manners are unstable; and of the adulteress likewise, because of shamelessness. Or this is the Church of the nations, which after washing through baptism says she has done nothing out of place. The righteous one is not “in youth,” since, perfected in a little, he filled long times. Such also is every adulterous woman—or a soul that alienated herself from the bridegroom, left her husband, and went after lovers.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The proverbs of Solomon are to be searched as riddles, so the wise ants are not the ants we see but those signified.
comments.comment: “There are four things that are least upon the earth, but these are wiser than the wise: the ants, who have no strength, who prepare their food in summer; and the rock badgers, a people not strong, who have made their homes in the rocks; the locust has no king, and marches in good order at a single word of command; and the lizard, which leans on its hands and is easily caught, dwells in the strongholds of a king” (Proverbs 30:24–28). But I do not use these words as though their meaning were plain. In keeping with the title (for the book is entitled Proverbs), I search into them as riddles. For it is the custom of these men to divide into many kinds the sayings that show one thing on their face and announce another in a hidden sense, and one of these kinds is the proverb. That is why in our Gospels too it is written that our Saviour said: “These things I have spoken to you in proverbs; the hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in proverbs” (John 16:25). It is not, then, the ants we see that are wiser even “than the wise” (Proverbs 30:24), but those that are signified, as it were, in the form of proverbs. The same must be said of the other animals.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Weaker souls flee to the rock on which Jesus founds the church, which is the confession of the faith.
comments.comment: But those souls that have arrived at this state and are weaker, called swine, flee to the rock upon which Jesus founds the church as an unconquerable fortress; and this is the confession of the faith. And in Proverbs it is said, 'And the swine, a people not strong, made their dwellings in rocks' (Prov 30:26). It is nothing wonderful that the rock is spoken of both singularly and plurally, meaning Christ who is simply the rock, and who is also spoken of as rocks according to various thoughts.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The locust is called kingless because it needs no leader, and these are those lightened by choice from earthly things.
comments.comment: Perhaps because we were not under a king before Christ’s kingship, the locust is called kingless. They have no leader as bees do; each one leads. These are those lightened by choice from earthly things, walking an ordered life. Or locusts are also those who want to fly by intellect yet cannot, and so climb only a little from the earth. But if they share in the practical life, they will be led into one practical rank.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the locust is said to have no king yet marches in order.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The locust is praised as orderly, obeying God's Word, and such is the Church.
comments.comment: “And she marches out from one command in good order.” The locust too is praised as orderly, obeying the command of God’s Word. Such is the Church: despised by people and compared to a locust as to living on the earth;…
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Leaders are both shepherds and lions, and all their subjects are to be brought to them as sheep and cattle.
comments.comment: The leaders of the peoples, who are shepherds of them both priestly and teaching-wise, turn out to be like sheep, while there are those presiding kingly rather than tyrannically as lions. And since both types of rulers are called shepherds and lions, it is necessary for all the subjects to be brought as sheep and other cattle, having a tendency toward the shepherds who graze, and toward the lions for the cattle. It has been said indeed in Proverbs: 'A lion is stronger than cattle, who does not turn away nor falls upon every cattle' (Proverbs 30:30).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The he-goat leading the flock stands for the one who leads Christ's people up toward the heights, or for Christ himself.
comments.comment: “And a he-goat leading a flock of goats.” Third is the he-goat—according to the Seventy alone—leading a goat flock, increasing and multiplying it and guiding it to pastures on the heights. No herd of animals climbs the high places like this. Such is the one who leads Christ’s people in the goat flock, raising them toward height. Otherwise the he-goat types Christ, offered for sin. To this one who is on high the whole multitude of the godly follows.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the he-goat of the verse as a leader raising his flock to the heights.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The goat leads the unpurified on the Savior's left.
comments.comment: And a goat is considered a scapegoat: if the unpurified are standing as rivals on the left side of the Savior, the goat leads these; lest the goat now signifies the devil.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The weak cannot teach rightly, and one drunk with the Master's house forgets his pains.
comments.comment: And the weak will not be able to judge rightly: they will not be able to teach rightly (Proverbs 31:5). Give drink to those in sorrows (Proverbs 31:5): he who is intoxicated by the potency of the master's house forgets his pains.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse about judging rightly and the drink given to those in sorrow.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Poor means lacking knowledge; weak means unpurified.
comments.comment: And distinguish between the poor and the weak: poor means one lacking in knowledge, and weak means the unpurified.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Bravery is the soul's mastery over its enemies, plundering what it has conquered.
comments.comment: What woman will find a brave one? Bravery is an excellent state of the rational soul, by which it has mastered the opposing forces of enemies. Such a thing will not be despoiled by dogs: having conquered the opposing power, we plunder it, learning the discourses concerning it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the valiant woman's strength as the courage of the rational soul.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The soul is dyed like wool and linen as it studies the discourses on living things, on practice and on nature.
comments.comment: Wool and linen being dyed: the soul is dyed like wool and linen, exercising itself in the discourses concerning the living and the non-living, or examining the discourses concerning the practical and the natural. And someone said that the soul is dyed like wool and linen, pulling the contemplation of bodies and incorporeal things toward it through the practical life.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The soul rises from the night to watch and pray, lest it fall into temptation.
comments.comment: And rising from the nights, she gave food to the household: the one who practices righteousness finds the soul rising from the night, being watchful; and certainly, also praying so that she might not fall into temptation; for she herself hastens to say, 'I awoke and became like a sparrow perching on a roof' (Psalm 102:7).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the woman who rises at night as the watchful, praying soul.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A pure mind is a lamp filled with spiritual contemplation, and a lampstand weaving virtue with virtue.
comments.comment: And her lamp is not extinguished through the whole night: a pure mind is a lamp, filled with spiritual contemplation. Her wicks are set in a lampstand: a pure mind is a lampstand, weaving virtue with virtue and doctrine with doctrine; or an articulated word, drawing spiritual contemplation from the mind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the lamp that is not put out as the pure mind.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The mind must correct what is within before it can go forth to the contemplation of the incorporeal.
comments.comment: Her husband does not care for those in the house when he lingers: the mind would not go forth, nor would it come to be in the contemplation of the incorporeal, without first correcting what is within; for the disturbance of the domestic affairs is accustomed to turn it back toward those from which it had departed; having acquired dispassion, it will linger in contemplation, and will not care for those in the house; for anger is clothed with gentleness and humility, and desire with temperance and self-control.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Words of earth and sea clothe the rational soul.
comments.comment: Clothing itself of deep color and purple: The words of earth and sea are garments of the rational soul from the depths and the purple.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The linen cloths go to the pure and the belts, which bind the passionate part of the soul, to the Canaanites.
comments.comment: He made linen cloths and gave them, but belts to the Canaanites (Proverbs 31:24): The linen cloth revealed on the roof (Acts 10:11) was a symbol of this sensible world; for the various animals contained therein showed the diverse characters of men, having been purified by the cross of Christ. If one linen cloth signified this world, perhaps many linen cloths contain the contemplation of various worlds, which the pure soul having contemplated, shared with others. If the Canaanites are interpreted as the lowly, it was not rightly that he gave the linen cloths to the lowly in mind, but rather the linen cloths to the pure, and to the Canaanites belts, which are symbols of practice, binding the passionate part of the soul.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The devil finds no rest in the pure soul, so its dwellings are secure, and lazy grain is wickedness.
comments.comment: Secure dwellings of its house: If the devil is king of all those in the waters and finds no rest through dry places, it is rightly said that the dwellings of the pure soul are secure. And he did not eat lazy grain: They say lazy grain is the grain of wickedness.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A soul that has wisdom rightly praises the fear of the Lord, which led it to such knowledge.
comments.comment: For a prudent woman is blessed (Proverbs 31:30), but let this one praise the fear of the Lord (Psalm 111:10): If the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, the soul which happens to possess wisdom rightly praises the fear of the Lord, which has become to her a precursor of such knowledge.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the wise woman is to praise the fear of the Lord.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus
